utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The Chamber will give its ruling on the accused's motion for suspension of proceedings. The Chamber has considered the arguments raised in the accused's motion for fourth suspension of proceedings filed on 2nd of February, 2011, and the Prosecution's response to that motion. According to the motion, the Prosecution disclosed 1.725 items, totalling an estimated 32.000 pages, and 152 videos containing an estimated 200 hours of material, to the accused on 31st January 2011. This material was disclosed on the basis that it may "fall within the ambit of Rule 68 or may be of relevance for the Defence case." The accused has requested a suspension of the trial proceedings for three months in order for him and his Defence team to review this newly-disclosed material. The Prosecution opposed the suspension, and, in the alternative, suggested the review of the disclosed material could be completed by the accused and his team in approximately one week. The Chamber recalls that an adjournment of the proceeding is an exceptional measure which it will only order if convinced that it is in the interests of justice to do so. It is satisfied that given the volume of material involved, the accused will require some time to review it and to determine whether and how to use it in these proceedings, and that it cannot be expected that this can be done while the trial continues. The Chamber, therefore, finds that it is in the interests of justice for the trial proceedings to be suspended for a period of six weeks to allow the accused and his team to prioritise their review of the disclosed material and incorporate it, if necessary, into his ongoing preparations for trial. It is regrettable that this is necessary, and we note that the impact of the Prosecution's continuing belated disclosure of Rule 68 material on the overall length on the trial with great concern. In reaching this conclusion, the Chamber is also mindful that the pattern of disclosure violations by the Prosecution has continued since the last suspension of proceedings in November 2010. Indeed, we are of the view that the Prosecution's response to this motion fails to give adequate weight to the importance of the Prosecution's obligation to disclose potentially exculpatory material as soon as practicable and the impact of the late disclosure of massive volumes of documents pursuant to Rule 68 on the accused's preparations and the smooth conduct of his trial. Turning to the timing of the six-week suspension, we do not consider it necessary for it to take effect as of 15th February, as requested by the accused. We are, instead, minded to continue hearing witnesses until the first week of March and to suspend proceedings thereafter. However, before deciding this finally, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to inform us, by the end of proceedings tomorrow, whether there are any specific witnesses who are scheduled to testify on particular dates in March or April or if there are any other matters to be factored into our decision on the precise date for the period of suspension. The Chamber will then issue a full written decision which will identify the specific dates when proceedings will be suspended and whether there will be certain dates within the period of suspension when witnesses will be heard. Having said that, shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And let us bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to express my gratitude for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, General. My apologies for the delay again. Today, we will be sitting until 4.30 in the afternoon, but the second break will be an hour for lunch instead, which will take place at 12.30. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, General. Yesterday, we agreed that the Bosnian side -- or, rather, the Muslim side launched its large-scale offensive, that they were firing at us from the total exclusion zone, and that the UN forces knew about that. Do you recall that when the agreement on the total exclusion zone was reached, the Serb side retained the right to take its weapons out and defend itself, and that that was regulated by the relevant protocol, and that was also recognised at each and every meeting that was held?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that in 1994, that something like that was in the agreement, yes. I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you that at meetings with Ambassador Akashi and with General Rose, as well as in the protocol itself, it was specified that if the United Nations cannot prevent or stop an attack that is already underway against the Serbs, the Serbs have the right to take their own weapons and defend themselves. Afterwards, they're supposed to return the weapons. My thesis is that that is something that is well known among the officers there, or, rather, the armed forces of the UN. Do you agree that you were aware of it too?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that there was this set of protocols. Again, without seeing them, I cannot recall the detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And there is no doubt that it referred to our right to take weapons from the weapon collection points, right, to take these weapons and to return them once the danger is over; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, without looking at the documents, I cannot recall the details of this arrangement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to look at the protocol briefly. D717, could we have that in e-court. Page 4 of this document, please. I believe that it's the second paragraph or the paragraph under number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please cast a glance. Do you agree that this unequivocally reiterates our right to use our weapons if the United Nations cannot ensure the observance of the zone by the Muslim side? Right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph am I being asked to agree to? I haven't read the whole document yet. That's why I'm asking which paragraph are we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 1.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, numbered "1"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it says that -- at the beginning, UNPROFOR -- that in the event of UNPROFOR withdrawing from the weapon collection points, which is what I think that is referring to, without the agreement of the BSA, or that it withdraws from its interposition areas between Serb and Muslim lines - that's the first set of conditions - the BSA reserves the right to redeploy its weapons. Again I'm assuming from the weapon collection points. While in the event of a Muslim attack on the Serbs which UNPROFOR is not able either to prevent -- either prevent or stop, immediately the BSA reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence. Now, I'm not clear from that whether, actually, it says, other than you can withdraw, redeploy weapons in the first set of that paragraph, whether that first bit applies to the second. But, yes, you have -- there is some form of agreement there in which, in those circumstances, you can start to take other actions of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see, in your book, which is 1D3196 [as interpreted], on page 10 -- in e-court, it's page 10; otherwise, it is page 346 and then it flows on to 347 of your book - that you understood that fully and that it is included in your book. Could we please see D3196 in e-court. Your book is, of course, "Utility of Force": [In English] "The NATO capability was subsequently used after a particularly murderous attack in early 1994 on the Markale Market Square in Sarajevo. The aim of the operation was to reinforce the safe area by declaring exclusion zones around it. Each zone was to be empty of all Bosnian Serb heavy weapons and, if not, would be attacked from the air. From the point of view of NATO, and in particular of US advocates of this idea, this was a simple proposition." [Interpretation] Can we now please see another page. The top of the next page, on the right: [In English] "... But from the UN and UNPROFOR points of view, such an action would be partial; it would also prevent the Bosnian Serbs from defending their people in, for example, their part of Sarajevo. These differences led to the two weeks ..." And so on. [Interpretation] So the first thing to be noted here is that it is understood that only the Serbian weapons would be re-deployed from the exclusion zone, and that was not the essence. The essence is that all the weapons should have been removed from the exclusion zone, but I can see that even you, in your book, completely understood that this was our right. Please have a look at this: [In English] "... the meetings went on and on." [Interpretation] It's in the middle. It says "years of service in NATO," and then it follows -- have you found that, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got to: "The meetings went on and on," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this passage which says that the meetings went on and on, but in the end the agreed result was another variant of the hostage and shield, as you call it, weapons would be collected at collection points and held under UN control, a word which you believe was open to interpretation, but the Serbs were able to maintain them in case they needed it for self-defence, in which case they would be returned, and so on. Would you agree that even though you were not there at the time, that we requested that this should be called "monitoring" rather than "control," and that that was accepted; namely, that the United Nations would be monitoring this? And the other thing, which is the most important, that it was clear to everyone that it was our right to use the weapons for self-defence; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the word -- the monitoring. I do recall, as I've said in the book and, I think, earlier -- no, I didn't say it earlier -- that the actual control was open to interpretation. So that may have -- the "monitoring" word may have appeared, for all I can recall. And, yes, there was a recognition that in -- for the need of self-defence, weapons could be withdrawn. Again, I don't recall under what arrangements this was to be done. It certainly would have involved the United Nations having some hand in releasing the weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would tender these two pages. But with all due respect, General, it was not envisaged that we should ask for permission. Once we were attacked and if the UN could not order them to stop, we were authorised to use our weapons. Can these two pages be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you're not giving evidence. You put your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking if this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it right that it was not envisaged that we should ask for permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- I just have to note, I mean, that wasn't in the guise of a question, it wouldn't have been transformed into a question without the Court's intervention, and there should be no pretense that those efforts at commentary are anything but. It's fine now if the -- upon the Court's urging, if that's translated into a question, the witness can deal with it as he wishes. But it should not be the constant burden of the Court or the Prosecution to monitor and point out its occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. General, could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll just refresh my memory as to -- no, again, I cannot the precise details, but I am -- I believe that there was some arrangement by which we would have been involved in the release of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have any objection to the admission of those two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1009, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in addition to the fact that the understanding was that only Serbs were supposed to remove the weapons, though the agreement implied all weapons, that in some places the rule was that only the Serbian side would be bombed if it violated this rule? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That in some places, the rule was that only the Serbian side would be bombed if it violated this rule." I don't think that was in any agreement at all. In theory, the exclusion zone applied to all sides, and there were weapon collection points for the Bosnian Army as well as the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me, General, that, so to speak, from your arrival to the area, you had a feeling that the bombing should take place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no feeling that it should take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the occasion of your arrival to the post as a commander, you had 20.000 soldiers who were subordinated to you and who were allowed to use force only for self-defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that in your documents and discussions, the possibility of bombing was already mentioned in the first week of April, and during the month of April, and especially during the first week of the month of May?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the probability of this occurring was becoming -- it was increasing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to have a look at another page from your book. It's 1D1396 [as interpreted]. It's page 7 in e-court. The previous document, 1D3196, and if we could have a look at page 7 in e-court, which is page 340 from the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph says: [In English] "But by the time I assumed command in 1995, there were some 20.000, the original deployment in 1992 was 5.000, all bound to their respective national headquarters and all prohibited from using force, except in self-defence, by the mandate of the Rules of Engagement." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that in spring 1995, first of all in May, but even before that, before the bombing of Serbian positions, the Serbian Army was defending itself from the Army of BiH, which had launched a large-scale offensive? It was precisely during that spring?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there had been two offensives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it happened that there was an opinion, and I could say that you had arrived with an intention to end the war, and in order to end it, that it was necessary to bomb the Serbs, and that the UN should change the mandate and be able to use force? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened -- I did not arrive with an intention to end the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But was your position that the United Nations should resort to force? The use of force, I mean.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not my position, and it certainly wouldn't have been one at all at the beginning of my tour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look -- or, rather, could this page 340 be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That page will be added to the previous portion; i.e., Exhibit D1009.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see page 15 in e-court of this same document, which is page 356 of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this to appear on the screen, General: In the first week of May, you said, and you repeated it in your statement and we shall come back to that, that you were under great pressure that the bombing should take place. Who was exerting this pressure?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was pressure from the NATO authorities, who were watching the circumstances in and around the exclusion zones. There were the demands from the Bosnian government in addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that was the reason why your first request to bomb the Serbs was refused at the command in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that was the reason. I deduced the reason -- wrong. I think the reason was connected with the -- with two factors: One, I'd started and had said, We don't want to do that, and then I had this apparent change of mind. And the second reason was, I think, to do with the politics in NATO and the UN at the time, but I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please turn your attention to the last passage in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I should have risen earlier and should -- and I will be asking, as a general matter, for references, specific references to page numbers of any document or statement in which it's asserted something was said. So could I just have the page reference or paragraph reference number to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Refusal from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The reference to pressure in the witness's statement that was the predicate for this series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the page number of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can withdraw this question temporarily and we'll come back to it with a document. But can I turn your attention to the last paragraph on page 356, General, beginning with the words: "By the time I arrived ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "By the time I arrived in the theatre, it appeared that the media unanimously ..." Do you want me to go on? How far do you want me to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, since everybody can read it, you can just give us your comments.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the whole paragraph, onto the next page, or just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This page.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This page, right. Yes, I think that was the situation at the time with the media, and an explanation of why -- well, beginning of the explanation of why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at page 357, lines 11 or 12: "Given this background, I sought to establish ..." [In English] "Given this background, I sought to establish a clear media policy as soon as I arrived in theatre, as with the use of force it seemed to me the key lay in the ability to escalate." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes, and that's what I thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can these two pages be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, those will be added to Exhibit D1009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these preparations to use force, and in such a way, at that, namely, that there can even be an escalation, was the basis of your preparation for using force against one side only; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm -- the reference to the preparations to use force is a reference to what is in evidence already? I didn't see it in that passage, and I don't recall the witness referring to it earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, be cautious when paraphrasing the previous answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we are going to see that paragraph now. We're going to have it called up. But before that, I would like to hear the witness's answer. I believe that is fully legitimate, that I put the question and then I give proof of what I have been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you started preparations for the effective use of force against one side, at that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- I am confused. You have given me a paragraph to read about my policy towards the media. I don't see that that's got anything to do with the use of force. In writing in this paragraph, I allude, I think, to an earlier discussion in this book about the theoretical background to the use of force, in which I explain about escalation, and I don't see that anything in this has to do with one side or the other of this unfortunate conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, right here in this paragraph, it says: [In English] "... as with the use of force it seemed to me the key lay in the ability to escalate." [Interpretation] But that is not only related to the media. It has to do with the entire attitude towards the warring parties and also these preparations to use force against one side only. Let me help you. Let's look at paragraph 96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's another statement of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 2686. It's your amalgamated statement. Page 24, paragraph 96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have a hard copy of his amalgamated statement? General, do you like to have that statement before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would help, yes, if it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your preparation, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's coming up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 24 now, paragraph 96. We have it in e-court too: [In English] "Late April/early May, we got the Joint Commission Observers in Srebrenica. These JCOs had been included, if I recall correctly, in the COHA at the end of 1994 as part of the observer and control mechanisms of that agreement. I would have been involved in the process of sending them in. They were valuable to me for communications and their ability as forward air controllers. As it got harder and harder to communicate with the enclaves, it was more important that I had a reliable form of communication with them, so I deployed JCO teams into Srebrenica and Gorazde. NATO nations had forward air controllers in their units who were practiced and certified to operate with NATO air forces, and this is where the JCOs were drawn from."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the end of April and the beginning of May, as soon as the JCOs were established, were you not thinking straight away that you needed these forward air controllers and that that was a preparation for the bombing that would ensue?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I wanted to get, as it said in this document, the JCOs into Srebrenica for the two reasons; for air control, tactical air control party or forward air controllers, and for communications. The -- it was certainly -- they were certainly there to be able to control aeroplanes, and I was making sure I was capable of doing that in all the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the United Nations forces were in our country on the basis of our own consent, and that that had been a prerequisite for their presence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that was the -- their original deployment was covered by that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that any change in the mandate would have to be given our approval so that we would accept you as a neutral presence? Is this not a change in your mandate, given these forward air controllers and preparations for an attack against one side only, the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not evidence of that at all. If you read the rest of the paragraph, you'll see why I wanted to put the JCOs there. And the reason was that the forward air controllers with the Dutch unit were no longer current because they hadn't been able to practice and maintain their certification with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So then you asked NATO to bomb the Serb positions. You are the commander of UNPROFOR, and you're preparing forward air controllers, and that meant the involvement of the UN forces into a conflict with the Serbs. As you say in your text, moving on from confrontation into conflict; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how this is connected with the Srebrenica situation, because they -- there wasn't bombing there until much later in the year. Or is this question not connected with the previous?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to show here that you sent JCO teams to Srebrenica and Gorazde that were actually forward air controllers. They were not observers. They were capable of guiding NATO aircraft. There was bombing in Gorazde, later on in Srebrenica as well, and before that, in May, there were bombings in Pale and elsewhere. So this is my question: In that way, did you not bring together NATO and the UN in your very own person? You are asking for the bombing to take place, and your soldiers are forward air controllers for the NATO air force. Is that not this move from the state of confrontation with the Serbs into conflict with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the resolutions of the -- that followed on from the -- and gave the authority to the exclusion zones and the safe areas, I was part of the system that had been established to maintain the safe area and exclusion zones -- safe areas and exclusion zones. Part of that system included NATO. And, therefore, I made sure that I had the ability to control NATO aeroplanes for the close air support and self-defence of the NATO forces in those enclaves. And for that purpose, I deployed the necessary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understand this correctly, we never gave any kind of approval for any kind of NATO presence in the enclaves. Right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't a NATO presence. This was a United Nations presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 11, which is page 348 in e-court, can we have a look at that page of your book now and see what you say there. Yes, yes, the book. We need the previous document, 1D396; page 11 in e-court. It's 348, then, in the first half of the book. It's around line 10: [In English] "One is, in effect, negotiating by threatening or using force in confrontation, not conflict. Technically, both NATO and the United Nations were in confrontation with the Bosnian Serbs, but NATO was focused only on the Bosnian Serbs, whilst UNPROFOR was dealing with all sides ..." And so on. [Interpretation] So it is my position that from the very outset, it was the Serb side that was the target, and that the use of force was envisaged for the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Since we can see here that the General was aware of what NATO was doing, doesn't this paragraph show that you were aware of the fact that NATO had this one-sided orientation against the Serbs only?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, did this, in a way, become a personal conflict for you, too, that you had completely sided with one of the parties in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have a look at a few other paragraphs in this document. But before that, can I tender this page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That page will be added as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A bit of patience now, please, because I would like to show a few short paragraphs from your book. It is page 353 in the book, itself, but it is page 13 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 353: "In May ..." It's the last paragraph: [In English] "In May, I attempted to reinforce the exclusion zone around Sarajevo, which had been violated with the breakdown of COHA when the Serbs resumed shelling the city and withdrew some weapons from the agreed collection points. To this end, I used NATO to bomb Bosnian Serb ammunition supplies. Whilst I did not see this in such terms at that time, I was in a confrontation with Mladic over this ..." [Interpretation] Further on -- well, in a way, you were in this sort of personal conflict with Mladic, and it seems that, to a large degree, this had become personal. Right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word is "confrontation," not "conflict." And if you like, I will tell you what I think those two words mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, please, by all means, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A conflict is a fight, a battle, an engagement. A confrontation need not be violent at all. It is when you do not share the same outcome in your -- in the intentions that you are pursuing. Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my understanding of your distinction between these two concepts. Can we look at 354, the next page, which is 14 in e-court, and then I would like us to have a look at a few brief paragraphs. And, of course, I'm counting on having these pages that I'm quoting admitted eventually. 354, can we have that, please. And now we are going to see where this is. Line 5 from the top: [In English] "I put the threat into effect. I moved from confrontation to conflict." [Interpretation] Is that it? It is here where you crossed this border between confrontation and conflict by bombing the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I've written there, and that is what happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we NOW also have a look at another passage from the same page. Just a second so I can find it. Lord Owen is mentioned. It's the upper half of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see "Lord Owen": [In English] " ... I had lost a battle or confrontation. In thinking this through, I came to the conclusion that I had to understand the use of force in a different way; that it had to be applied to alter a decision-maker's mind, and that this understanding must affect my choice of targets." [Interpretation] And then let us have a look at page 18 in e-court. It is page 362 of the book, but it's near the top: [In English] "... but as the lady said, you can't be a little bit pregnant, and you can't be a little bit interventionist either. If you stand in the middle of someone else's fight, you must expect to be pushed around. And if you do intervene, decide if you are fighting one or all of sides and get on with it."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the page before 362, page 361, to see how that paragraph is actually situated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "... but if there was any doubt about the matter, the directive issued to me by the NATO in late May -- by the UN in May, clarifying that the safety of forces was more important than implementing the mandate."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the other page be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it follow from this that you did take sides in the civil war?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. You're forgetting that I am reacting to a set of circumstances that I haven't created. There are two parties in a confrontation and a conflict, and this one was even more complex because -- as you pointed out, it's a civil war, so there's another set of confrontations and conflicts going on at the same time. And the last bit of the book you showed me, where I'm doing the thing about "can't be a little bit pregnant," is a reflection on the events after the -- it's a lesson I'm drawing from these events. It isn't the -- it isn't necessarily how I'm thinking about it on the day in, for sake of argument, May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do I understand properly, General, that there were levels of intervention? The first was the close air support, the close support which was envisaged as assistance to units which were under attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. You reacted, and that was one of the reactions in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that General Mladic told all commanders, If my forces attack you, please feel free to respond, and I will accept that; no one must attack you, you are free to respond? Are you aware of this position of his?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no, but it may have been said to one of my predecessors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right. The next was a punitive measure, the so-called air-strikes. So air-strikes are not close air support, they're a punitive measure; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are punitive and reactive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if a cannon or a tank happens to be in a place where it must not be, it will then be fired on; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not automatically, but it could have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the bombing which took place in May was neither the close air support nor an air-strike against a disobedient piece of weaponry, but it was strategic bombing with the aim of diminishing the Serbian defence power; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was -- the requirement was to re-establish the exclusion zone and to see the weapons that had been removed from the weapon collection points back in the weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did not bomb the weapons which were not returned, but an ammunition depot, and yesterday you said that that changed matters once you destroyed such an amount of ammunition; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons that target was chosen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on you say, on page 76, that the aim was also to intimidate Pale, because the ammunition depot was right next to Pale?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 76 in the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's the page of the transcript. 76 is the page of the transcript of yesterday's session.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah-ha. I don't think I used the word "intimidate." I think I said that it could be heard or seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, to leave an impression. That was what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And also you believed that the Serbs should return the weapons they had taken in order to defend themselves. Would you agree that weapons are not returned in the midst of an offensive, that the offensive was not over yet and that the conditions for returning the weapons had not been met yet? And, excuse me, it's not recorded in the transcript that the witness confirmed what I asked him, that he said, Okay, in response to my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the General confirmed with the word, leaving an impression. Can you proceed to answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The requirement that I had placed and why I had requested NATO to conduct the bombing was for those weapons to be returned. It was -- and they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did the Muslims -- but we'll come back to that later. 10

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see another section of the book. Can this page be admitted first or can I count on it that all the pages that we will present would be attached or, rather, added to the exhibit which is already admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done. So far, pages 353 to 354, and pages 361 to 62 will be added.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 358 is also something we had a look at, or, rather, we'll do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you decided to intervene. And after the crisis with the bombing, you decided to introduce another formation called "Rapid Reaction Forces"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't -- they weren't called that at that stage. During that crisis, I started to form a reaction force, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see page 358. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The RRF," that's how it begins. It's the fourth line from the top: [In English] "The RRF was to be commanded by a French brigadier general with a multinational headquarters. Subsequently, Britain deployed an airmobile brigade to the Dalmatian coast, and this, too, was available to me on request. The force was not to adopt the UN blue helmets or paint their vehicles white; it was an unmarked UN force. This was fine by me. They were to fight, and I did not want them to look like the UN. I particularly wanted the guns. In comparison with aircraft, guns with the appropriate target-locating and fire-control systems apply fire as accurately, can maintain the fire for longer, are not weather dependent, and would be under my command. They could, in the right quantities and deployment, defeat the Bosnian Serb artillery." [Interpretation] So you envisaged that they would not look as the United Nations, and you wanted to have adequate weapons under your control so that you could defeat Serbian artillery; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in the United Nations, they were not too enthusiastic about these ideas, namely, that the United Nations should be turned into one of the warring parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They accepted the use of this force. It was part of the United Nations. There was an argument about having it or not, but, nevertheless, that's what they decided in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also without our agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask for this page to be admitted -- actually, to be added. And could we now please have look at 1D395 -- 1D3195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That page will be added.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3195, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is your interview dated the 12th of January, 2000 - page 8, paragraph 30 - which you gave to the Dutch Institute. Please have a look at this paragraph: [In English] "Smith was still upset because of the fact that the UN did not allow him to bring artillery to Sarajevo. The British had the artillery, but it had to stay on ships in the Adriatic and could not be used on land on orders from the UN. Artillery would have been more useful than aeroplanes." [Interpretation] So there was no enthusiasm about your action, your preparations to fight against the Serbs by using artillery and Rapid Reaction Forces. The British artillery decided to remain on ships. Did you get the artillery that you had asked for eventually? Did you get it so that you could overpower the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I want to go back to this document you've shown me and the paragraph 30 on page 8. It refers -- that refers to my time in the Ministry of Defence in London, and I think the year in question is 1993. And it's a discussion -- or what occurred was that there was the potential to deploy artillery with the initial British battle group in that year after some incident in the vicinity of Tomislavgrad, and that's what that paragraph is referring to. It's got nothing to do with my time as a UN commander some years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But obviously your position at the time was already that artillery should be introduced on your side into this civil war; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct in those terms. The -- my position was that if you are faced by artillery attacks, which was the case in this particular deployment, and you wish to defend yourself, then you should take some artillery with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please have a look at the following passage, which says -- the next passage, 31 -- can we please move on to page 9. Please have a look at what is here, and then let us show page 9 and have a look at what's on top of that page. It says here that both the Muslims and the Croats opposed this because they were afraid that this force could be used against them as well. Is this an excuse, after all, that the Muslims and Croats were afraid of the Rapid Reaction Forces because you had made them aware earlier that you were partial to them, that you were on their side, and that the conflict -- that you had been in conflict with your superiors before because of this partiality of yours; isn't that correct? Was it practically possible that the Muslims would be punished by use of weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was perfectly possible for that to happen should such a situation -- such a situation occur that would require that reaction. And I'm -- I don't see how you're making the linkage that I had made them aware that I was partial to them. The whole of that paragraph 31 in the document that you've referred to me is concerning the Rapid Reaction Force and my arguments as to why I only wanted it if I could use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you came into conflict with your superiors about your will to use force?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confrontation, perhaps, but not conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at page 4 of this document, paragraph 12, then. Here, your confrontation with General Janvier is mentioned about the use and deployment of helicopters for supplying the enclaves, and so on; is that correct? You say here: [In English] "It was the only time that Smith and Janvier disagreed. Smith said that at a certain point, the young Turks in Zagreb turned against Janvier because they agreed with Smith. They, too, were in favour of the use of force, as opposed to Janvier." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written there. And I should make the point, from this paragraph, that the argument between General Janvier and I was about the interpretation of our orders, as opposed to the use of force, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the "young Turks" means, figuratively, radicals, those who were ready to fight; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those were -- there had been a leak of some documents showing my position, and those were the people I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were slowly creating the conditions for a conflict with Serbs, and you were even happy about this conflict; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was creating the conditions so that I could react effectively, if I needed to, with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have a look at the document 1D3196, page 18 in e-court. It's page 363, and I will read it, and we'll find it. It's somewhere -- page 18 in e-court. It's fine, we have it here on the screen. It's page 363 of the book, and close to the top of the page, it says the following: [In English] "Having made the threats, we could be sure Mladic would take measures to counter it. I explained I was quite happy to fight the Bosnian Serbs." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or anyone else, for that matter. It's my profession, or was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us now take a look at page 20 in e-court, which is two pages on. It's page 366 of the book. And, again, I'm interested in a passage which is close to the top of the page. [In English] "I did not want the Serbs to have the initiative ..." [Interpretation] It's the first paragraph that begins on this page: [In English] "In essence, I wanted to be the one who chose when and where we fought, and what about, and so the preparations continued. We made plans for what we would do for attacks on each of the safe areas, and the Rapid Reaction Forces continued to deploy, always making itself look as much as possible like part of NATO. In parallel, we had been slowly reducing the size of the British contingent in Gorazde ..." [Interpretation] And so on. So you were preparing for a fight against the Army of Republika Srpska, and you withdrew your British soldiers from Gorazde so that they wouldn't be taken prisoners; correct.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wouldn't be used as hostages. That was the reason for removing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And further on you say --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both page 363 and 366 will be added to the book exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you managed to be more clever than Mladic about Gorazde, because he promised to you that in case of crisis, UNPROFOR would be allowed to pass through our territory in peace with all weapons, under the conditions that it did not leave the weapons to the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the arrangement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you certainly didn't tell him that the crisis would occur when you entered into a war with his troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that that would be the crisis. I was going to be withdrawing those people anyhow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at your statement, the amalgamated statement, page 50. You have it with you, and I'm interested in paragraph 197.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the withdrawal take place on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph were you referring to? I'm sorry. 197?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it is. We have it on the screen now, 197. On the 25th of August, you began preparations by having a meeting with Mladic to withdraw your soldiers from Gorazde; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see the passage. Let us not read it. Is it the same August during which the Markale II incident happened as well as the bombing?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is it the appropriate time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if it is convenient. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, General, it seems to me that already on the 25th, on the 25th of August, you knew that a crisis was in the making, and that's why you took your soldiers out; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd been trying to remove people from the -- these exposed positions for some time. I think you'll find that much earlier in the month, if not before, we've been telling everybody that the British were not going to replace their people in Gorazde, and nor were the Ukrainians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But at the time, you already knew -- or, actually, you took part in making the plans for using force against the Army of Republika Srpska, and what was being awaited was just a good opportunity; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a question of waiting for the opportunity. It was the question of waiting for the event to occur. We had to have an attack on a safe area first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D3196, your book, can we have a look at that again. It is page 20 in e-court, and in the book it is 367. It's around the middle of 367: [In English] "So in the end ..." [Interpretation] Line 12 or 13: [In English] "So in the end, the decision taken at the London Conference came down to this: If I was to use the forces available to me, NATO and the Rapid Reaction Forces to the best effect, I had to seize the first opportunity presented by an attack on Sarajevo and, if at all possible, ignore attacks on the other safe areas. Having done the planning with NATO, I was aware there were only so many targets suitable for the attack. The more we could mix the mode of attack - air, artillery and the battleground - the greater our options and effect; by a wide margin, this was achieved best around Sarajevo. My Rapid Reaction Forces was an ad hoc force ..." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] So the opportunity arose for Sarajevo, at that. While planning, it was Sarajevo that people had in mind, whereas the other safe areas were outside your planning altogether. So the opportunity arose on the 28th of August; right.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Plans were made for all the safe areas. The point was that I could execute the plans -- the best plan to execute was the one around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the last paragraph in the book [as interpreted]. It says that a shell fell, and that was the opportunity; right: [In English] "The Serbs were already claiming it was nothing to do with them, and that the Bosniaks had fired on their own people, but there was no evidence to support this contention. Nonetheless, I --"

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same page, the last paragraph. 367: [In English] "On the 28th of August ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see it, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't start reading from the very beginning of the paragraph. But further on, you say: "Nonetheless, I wanted to establish ..." [In English] " ... beyond a reasonable doubt that the shells were fired from Serb territory before our attack was initiated. General Janvier was on leave at the time, and the key was mine to turn." [Interpretation] Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and that this -- this incident was the -- required me to react to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the decision to bomb the Serbs, you made it on the 28th of August, in the evening; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me -- I think it was that date, yes, but it may have been -- it was certainly in the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this page be admitted, added to that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, these two pages will be added.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to the amalgamated statement. The number is -- you have a hard copy. Please look at page 52, paragraph 202 [as interpreted]: [In English] "I made the decision with Cincsouth to initiate a bombing campaign as a response to this shelling." [Interpretation] It is paragraph 203. The transcript says "202."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the evening of the 28th, as is written here, you made the decision to initiate the bombing campaign; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. It would have been later on that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know what time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a look at paragraph 200 on page 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that two teams investigated the site of the incident; isn't that right? One was an UNMO team, and the other was a team from Sector Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in the same paragraph, you say: [In English] "The UNMOs automatically carried out an investigation and recorded the data they collect. So there were two sets of investigations. Investigations took place with a slightly different set of competency. Between these two, we found ourselves with a certain amount of disagreement as to what had occurred. None of these investigations concluded that the killing shell had come from Bosnian positions, but there were two different views as to the direction the rounds came from." [Interpretation] Let us now see what the conclusion of the UNMO team was. Paragraph 207 now, page 52. Then we have to move on to 53: [In English] "At 1823 hours on the same day, Mladic reported to me that the results of his investigations concluded that no BSA forces were involved in the attack on Markale Market. I informed him that the UNMO investigation was progressing slowly, but they had established that the round responsible for killing the victims was a 120-millimetre mortar round probably fired from the south." [Interpretation] Is that correct? 1823, this is the conversation between you and Mladic, according to this paragraph of your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, and I think that's what happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the 28th of August, at 1900 hours, UNMOs held a meeting with the Muslim police. Can we have P150. Page 2, page 2 of 150. Towards the very bottom of page 2, this is what it says, paragraph 3. I'm going to read it out now: "The investigation team tried very hard to prove that the attack came from the Serb side, due to the normal use of heavy mortars, that is likely, but there is no hard proof on this fact."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, 40 minutes after your conversation with Mladic, the investigation team cannot establish, despite of their wish and effort to blame the Serbs, that it had actually come from the Serb side; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he has written there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same document, if we look at number 2 -- I believe that is page 1. Can we go back to the first page of this document. The bearings, in combination of the estimated angle of impact, could give no evidence on the origin of fire, since it is not known with which charge the projectile had been fired; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the 28th of August, in the evening, you had no way of knowing beyond a reasonable doubt that this incident in Markale was caused by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date, again, and time of this UNMO report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was the meeting on the 28th at 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that time, the -- in my headquarters, we have other sources of reporting, and I can't recall the exact flow of the -- and what order these reports came. And I would not have seen that particular one, either, the one up on evidence at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One of the two investigations, General, 40 minutes after you informed Mladic that it had probably come from the south, says that the site from where it was fired cannot be established. But let's move on. The next morning, on the 29th of August at 10.00, you said to General Mladic that it was established beyond reasonable doubt that the incident in Markale II was the doing of the Serbs. This sounds like a conclusion of a full criminal investigation that leaves no doubt whatsoever and that does not involve any further investigations. Isn't that what you informed him of? Let me help you. Let's have a look at the amalgamated statement, paragraph 208 on page 53. Can we have the previous document, the amalgamated statement, page 53, paragraph 208. Please have a look. At 1000 hours, you said to Mladic that it was established beyond reasonable doubt; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that it was beyond reasonable doubt that the shells had come from BSA territory and that the firing point was some three and a half to four kilometres south-west of the impact point, and this was a result of my own investigation that I was required to make in order to make the decisions that were required of me of the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the position of the United Nations? Who carried out this investigation that you relied upon?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNMOs and forces -- and people drawn from the forces under my command. And the position of the United Nations was that as a result of the London Conference, the decision as to whether or not to turn the key rested with the military commanders, and at that time I was the military commander with that decision to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to that, but let us see what the position of the UN was. Can we have P0 -- or, rather, P906. It's a telegram that was sent at 10.36 on the 29th of August, 1995, by General Janvier to Kofi Annan. At that time, he was head of peace operations. The 29th of August, at 10.36. Please look at the date. "UN restricted," and so on and so forth. So it is Annan who is sending this telegram. And now let us look at page 3, "Sector Sarajevo": [In English] "The sector has become very intense with a moderate level of firing incidents (1.746 recorded). The most active areas were in Nedzarici, Igman, airport, Mojmilo and Grbavica." [Interpretation] By the way, General, Nedzarici and Grbavica, are they Serb neighbourhoods within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grbavica, was, yes. At least I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nedzarici, as well, if you recall. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these things that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "At 11.10, five 120-millimetre mortar shells impacted down-town. One mortar impacted in Markale [B/C/S spoken], killing over 30 persons and injuring more than 80 others. This mortar shell was assessed to be fired from 170 degrees magnetic. Investigation to determine the distance to the firing point is ongoing. The definition of firing positions for mortar rounds is very difficult, as it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles." [Interpretation] So at 10.00, you informed Mladic that it is beyond any reasonable doubt, and your commander, General Janvier, 40 minutes after you, says that that is not the case; that it was not established, that it cannot be established?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot account for what is going on in the headquarters above me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the position of the United Nations; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've shown me is a report from my superior headquarters. I don't know that that's got -- gives you any idea of the position of the United Nations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see what you say in your amalgamated statement. Page 51, paragraph 201. You say the Cymbeline radar failed to pick up the trajectory of any shell. Let us see -- can you read that part that starts with: "The Cymbeline radar covers an arc ...," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that the Cymbeline radar failed to pick up the trajectory of any shell in a built-up area: [In English] "If you want to fire a mortar at a short range, you must fire it at a high trajectory which would have crossed the arc. So these shells must have been fired from far away from the confrontation line and at a lower trajectory." [Interpretation] That was your conclusion; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was part of that investigation, the conclusions from that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us leave aside the fact whether you can fire using mortars in such mountainous terrain and in that way. We're going to prove that some other way. However, your investigation did not prove that that is actually how this happened. So let us look at P1445 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, in the meantime, did you report to the headquarter in Zagreb about your own investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure I must have had a telephone conversation or two. But because General Janvier was on leave at the time, and because I had the key, and because the decision now lay with the military, not with the political authorities, I suspect I was doing -- I was not doing a great deal of informing my superiors at the time, since the decision lay with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at this document, paragraph 2 on page 3 -- actually, the last page of this document. We see what the document is. It has already been admitted. The last page, paragraph 2, "Cymbeline": [In English] "Cymbeline radar was operating, but the elevation of the antenna was higher and would have detected, hence, in a higher trajectory. At least several of the five rounds would have been detected if fired close to the confrontation line. If fired from a longer range, the arc of trajectory would most likely have been below the beam of the Cymbeline radar; thus, not detected ." "Most likely." [Interpretation] "Most likely," what does that sound like to you? Does it sound like "beyond reasonable doubt"?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used the words "most likely." And while it is not an absolute positive, it is most likely to be positive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now show a diagram that will show what it was like. Can we have 1D2830. We're not tendering it. We'd just like to have it displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember that the angle of descent was 67 degrees?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the angle of descent, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a variation of an objection that has been raised before in connection with similar efforts. This document is about to be put to the witness as if it reflects facts established, from which questions can be posed. We don't know the provenance of this document. I think that's why it hasn't been tendered previously. It appears to be, as we understand -- as I understand these documents, compilations assembled by someone associated with the Defence. On what basis, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since the Defence is allowed to put his case to the witness, so we'll allow him to proceed. But I'm not sure whether the General is an appropriate one to be asked about these questions. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to tender it now. We'll do it later with someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is, General: In view of the mountainous terrain, in view of the fact that it was a built-up area, do you see that the calculations show that under an angle of 67 degrees, the trajectory would have been higher if the distance was greater, not lower? This is a graphic display of the range tables, with variations for different charges, from plus 1 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this question seems to embrace a combination of the concerns that I expressed and the concern the Court expressed; that is, it asks the witness, who is, as the Court indicated, is not the appropriate person to render opinions about this document, which implicates the concerns I expressed before. So it is inappropriate for several reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have heard evidence to the effect that the trajectory must have been low. In light of that evidence, the Defence -- the accused is entitled to put the question whether, in view of the mountainous terrain and in view of the fact that it was a built-up area, that the trajectory would have been higher if the distance was greater, not lower. Can you answer the question, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer it from the evidence put on the screen, but I make the point that the comparison being made is with the Cymbeline arc and the trajectory of the round. I -- it's not a question of the range of the -- the range table that you have displayed here. I don't -- it could easily have been on that -- I don't -- I can't answer the question against the investigations that we were carrying out and use that range table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The basic issue is a logical one, a general issue. Do you still claim that the greater the distance, the lower the trajectory, or is it the other way around, which is our theory, by the way?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this chart, which I don't fully understand or recognise, that's what this chart is showing, but I'm not sure that's correct or needs to be correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's according to the firing tables, but we'll deal with it later. Can we see 1D2231 to see how this looks in relation to the Cymbeline beam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is it, General. With a 0 plus 1 charge, this shell could cross the beam that was set as 548 metres. Any higher charge would certainly have been picked up. Do you agree that the radar would have covered anything beyond 548 metres, anything coming from above that level?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I don't want this to get confused with the Defence's obligation to put its case, not merely the right to do so, but this -- I recall this particular exhibit. I recall it was objected to, I think, at least twice by Mr. Gaynor. The Court understood the basis for that objection, it was upheld, and I'm surprised to see it pop up again, particularly in this context. It was rejected in the context of presentation to experts who would have been in a better position to grasp the problems with the document, but as was noted earlier, there's -- there were questions about not only the document's provenance but the premises upon which it was based. I don't think we should be seeing constant efforts to circumvent the Court's earlier ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, my understanding is that the accused is now putting his case, and this document is being used as an aid to explain the situation or what he has in mind. So on that basis, allow him to proceed. And I wonder whether the General would be able to answer the question, having understood that situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, and I don't understand the chart. I don't -- it's not really clear to me, what's being said, and I don't think I can help the Court. The -- apart from the fact that this is some 16 years before this investigation took place, the business of the radar, and the trajectory was part of the investigation. It wasn't the investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We won't be tendering this now, Your Excellency, but it's just as you understood it. I was just trying to elicit the witness's opinion to his best ability. Let's see what you said in paragraph 200 of your statement, page 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 200: [In English] "Because the attack was so significant ..." [Interpretation] We can go back to -- for the other participants, we need the next page: [In English] "Because the attack was so significant, I wanted to be absolutely sure that all the data had been collected, and so I had a second iteration of this investigation in which my senior intelligence officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Powers, was instructed to collect all available data from other sources ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. I would like to ask you for a specific explanation which you seem not to have taken into consideration, and we'll look at it now. And I beg all parties for a little indulgence. It will take 12 to 13 minutes. 1D2838, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "It's just a -- first of all, I want to introduce myself. I'm Colonel Demurenko, Chief of Staff Sector South Sarajevo. But really today, it's not important, because I'm like -- only not like chief of staff, but like citizen of my country and like a professional military man, colonel. I want to explain any details of investigation which was provided UN -- so-called UN expertise about very terrible events which were a few days ago. As you know, it was Visoko, in down-town, when, after explosion of mortar, mortar shell, on 10 Central Street of the city, that after what was approximately 35 people died and more than 80, in accordance with the report, wounded. And as a professional man, I cannot agree with argument of UN specialist about reasons and sources of this shelling. It is absolutely unacceptable for me and for my military friends in this area, consent of this argument, and therefore I will try to explain any new details which I know. "Firstly, if you know, the main serious facts for us is following. This is the material -- maybe one portion of all material of UN specialist about this shelling. This is a shoot report with -- it's entered on French language, but with a very strange conclusion. This conclusion include idea about this shelling was from Serbian side, I mean Bosnian Serbs. "This is a small picture which explained angle on the street, Marsal Tito, and angle which was between ground and shell, mortar shell. It's very important for us. I will explain it following, afterwards. "This is a copy of photo pictures of this place. This is a street. This is a place where it is exploded of the shell. "This is very important for us, showing a picture. As you can, this is direction of fire [indicates], this is place of explosion [indicates]. And in accordance with the investigation, direction of fire was 176 degrees, or in accordance with the French custom, 2976 mils. Really, this is the south-east area. It's very important for us also. "This is a picture about -- it's very interesting. This material of Bosnian police, I mean government Bosnian police. It's about angle between ground and shell. As you can see, 70 degrees. "And last paper is really -- this is a small slice of copy from map. "And this is my idea, which I can explain all this paper. "In accordance with this material, I believe that specialists which was participated in this investigation was very professional and honest people. And so, therefore, in accordance, once again, with this official investigation and material, we have any picture. It's symbolic. You know, this is Sarajevo [indicates], this is the confrontation line, green [indicates]. This is the two building and place where is explode, this shell [indicates].
