In accordance with this material, direction of fire was 100 -- 106 degrees. In accordance with another material, it's once again very interesting question why, in UN, we have two different material of investigation, but not different, and one conclusion. But in accordance with another material of investigation, they said about another angle. "About first, once again, we know what was used. It's a 120-millimetres mortar shell. It's a former Yugoslavia weapon, and before it, it was Soviet system. I know it very well because I'm field commander, like a professional soldier. Many times, I participated in real, practical shelling and managed them; I mean, my artillery officers. "In accordance with the main documents for this system, this is a table with whole data about characteristics of this system. We can see that for this system, normally used six standard charge -- charges, charges. And in accordance with this angle, 70 degrees, and this is the direction 176, we can, after comparison with the standard data, see on following map. First explosion, it could be in accordance with this, once again, this degrees and this degrees [indicates]. In this area [marks], 900 metres. Next, in this area [marks], this is really 1.400. Next, 2.000 [marks]. Really, this is on confrontation line. Theoretically, it could be from Serbian, theoretically. I will, once again, explain it. And the next three [marks] are the 2.700, 3.400, and the last charge they can use for 3.600. "Today, personally, with my special -- not special, very small investigation group, including artillery officers, we was on this place [marks], this place [marks], this [marks], this [marks], and this [marks], really by my [indiscernible], and I can affirm absolutely, without -- or beyond any doubts, this is place unacceptable or unsuitable for firing position, mortar shell. No perspective, stay on this position and shell to this area. And therefore, conclusion of material of investigation was wrong. "Now I said only about terrain where is located Serbian troops, and special without my proposals about this area. This is not my job. I'm soldier, I'm colonel, and this is a business for special group like -- maybe for this group necessary include criminal persecutors, members of court-martial, I don't know. Maybe it's a ballistics person and so on and so on. So really, for us, it's necessary understand it, that it was wrong. "About another direction, this is the distance between place of explosion and place of fire position was 2.100 metres [marks]. Same, I was here today, absolutely no perspective locate firing, battery, or platoon, or even one mortar for this area, because this is a really rock slope and forest, and no perspective fired from this position. I can affirm it, and I will have today a photo picture about each of these places. "I can show for you also a map with exactly direction -- one, this direction [indicates], and another alternative direction, and I think the most problem for official investigation group was following: They investigate only angles and directions, and automatically thinking about Serbian so-called aggressions against civil population in Sarajevo, but I think it's not correct. You agree with me. It's necessary more deep investigation. We can organise ballistic expertise, for example, from this place [indicates] or from all place on this area, and we can use the smoke shell for identification place where is exactly can locate this fire position. "And maybe now not necessary more detail explanation, because I have no time enough for this. But, once again, I want statement that it was wrong material, it was absolutely bad conclusion, not correct, and subsequences of -- or the consequences of this event is very bad, because this is Sarajevo. Around Sarajevo, you can listen sound of shelling, and yesterday we had air-strikes around this area. Every hour, civilian people and military personnel is wounded and died. I think it is absolutely unacceptable, especially unacceptable for professional military personnel. "We cannot agree when we following after any strong group and no chance explain our separate point of view. We have it, separate point of view. And, once again, I am not like a citizen of my country. I must said let's stop them, stop false and falsehood and lie about Serbian aggression in this area. And especially -- especially - I stressed on that - I don't speak about Bosnian terrain. It's not my business. I don't want accuse against somebody or anybody. This is a problem for professional criminalists [sic], not for us. But for us, necessary every time repeat, please -- or investigate it absolutely correctly, with full argumentation, or stop it, and stop all type of action, I mean UN, NATO and so on, against this country. "And also I want to speak on -- few words on my native language, because I think it's necessary explain why -- more preferable for me, American mass media and mass media of Russia. "In USA, I had few years ago my military education. I love really this country, and I believe that this country can support all type of activity and military peacekeeping in this country."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your patience and your attention. I would like to thank all the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this Colonel Demurenko visited all putative potential firing positions. Did you visit any of those locations before making your decision?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you include in your report this opinion from Colonel Demurenko, who is also the chief of the Sarajevo staff?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the deputy commander of the Sector Sarajevo, and he was holding the report that was produced by Sector Sarajevo as part of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Considering that he's a very experienced artilleryman and a professional soldier, did you somehow take his opinion into account when writing your report about this incident?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not directly. He was in the subordinate headquarters, and I had their report. And I think he is reporting some days -- or this television thing you showed us is some days after I've actually made the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it seems that was a day later. Is it the case that he had to hold this press conference because his report could not find its way to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I remember him doing this. I -- but no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who decided that his report should not be forwarded or should not be built into your report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem his report is after I've already made the decision. I was confident then and I am confident now that Sector Sarajevo, as a headquarters, conducted a proper investigation, and I can -- and I understand that he, as the deputy commander, would have had every opportunity to put his case in that investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this video-clip in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Based upon the witness's confirmation that Colonel Demurenko had this interview at the time, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1010, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us now see how you explained this episode with Colonel Demurenko in your report. 1D3198, please. That is an information report dated 28 August 2003, but it regards this incident. Can we see page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4: [In English] "There had been pressure from Admiral Smith to punish by bombing the Serbs. One of the two deputies in Sector Sarajevo was a Russian colonel who said that the mortars must have been fired from within the confrontation line. He argued that we didn't understand the nature of Warsaw Pact-sourced ammunition. Another theory was that the Bosnians fired a round in after the Bosnian Serbs. I didn't accept the argument that the Bosnians were shooting at their own people, without proof. There will always be conspiracy theories." [Interpretation] I believe it is praiseworthy that you don't want to accept anything without proof, but does that also apply to the Serbs, that nothing should be accepted without proof, even if it seems to indicate that the Serbs are to blame? What I was trying to ask, General, is that I can compliment you on needing proof to blame the Bosnians, but does it also apply to the Serbs? Do you need proof to blame the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I carried out this investigation, to decide whether or not -- wrong -- to decide who was responsible for putting these rounds into the market-place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what you told Mladic and how you informed him of the pressures you were under. Are you the kind of man who gives way under pressure, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is for others to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see in e-court 1D3171. This is a transcript of your conversation with General Mladic. Can we see page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see this bit where Mladic says: "It's therefore very important that a mixed commission visits the site immediately." [In English] "I am prepared to send two officers immediately, with General Smith's guarantee for their safety, to examine the entire situation on site and assess the case with representatives of the other side and UNPROFOR forces." [Interpretation] So Mladic is suggesting that the other side, the Muslim side, be also present, and you say: "All right." Then the General says: "As I have said before, I will see what can be done with this idea, but you will understand the pressure I'm under at this moment." And then Mladic goes: "I fully understand, and I would not want the General to succumb to pressure. But in the interests of peace, to contribute to clearing up this whole case ..." [In English] "... particularly because these forms of pressure on their own are very indicative and probably a part of a preconceived plan. I would not want to have anyone succumb to the atmosphere of pressure, but to examine the entire case properly and rationally, at the level of a mixed commission." [Interpretation] Could you now help us understand what kind of pressures you, in your high position, could have been before you made the decision to bomb the Serbs? Who -- who is the person who was able to exert pressure on you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- could I know which of those three telephone calls we're referring to here? Is this the first, or the second, or even the third?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think it was the first or the second. The third one was on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, so it's either the first or the second one. Do we know which one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can find out. Let's see the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It does not show the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we're on the 28th --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At night. The Prosecution may assist us, but I think it's the second one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This looks as though it's the first call.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he's saying -- I assume he's heard about it. He says he's only heard about it "five minutes ago."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, so it must have been at that time. That's your first conversation, and then you're looking for details. He's asking for time to ask his people. You say you already have reports from your people. And on page 3, we see that you said you were under pressure, and you were asking General Mladic to appreciate that. I'm now asking you to explain to the Trial Chamber who it was who was able to exert pressure on the UN force commander in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm using the phrase as much as a -- explaining the significance and importance of the situation, as much as personal pressures, as it were. Nevertheless, there was a pressure for me to make a decision that was required of me, if not now, very soon. The people in Zagreb, the Bosnian government, and a bit later, I think it was, the NATO headquarters in Naples are communicating me -- with me and asking me what I'm going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, Mladic is not asking you to do anything here. He's only asking you to conduct an investigation, and he's offering and suggesting a mixed investigative commission consisting of the UNPROFOR, the Muslims and the Serbs. Why was that unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was me, not a joint commission, that had to make this decision, in the first place. And, secondly, as I thought about it more, it was going to be impractical to carry it out because I didn't anticipate the Bosnian government would tolerate any -- a joint commission in this issue. But, primarily, this was a decision I had to make, and I was getting on with making it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Nobody's questioning that you were the one making decisions. This is only a question of investigation. Can this be admitted, this part of the transcript, or perhaps the entire transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification, following our practice?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1011.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D3196, please. That's a page from the book. Let us see what you wrote in your book about that. 1D3196. In e-court, it's page 21, and it's 368: [In English] "Mladic wanted a joint commission. I said we would have to consult my higher headquarters. I was stalling."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you actually ask your command, your superior command? Let's see what -- [In English] "I'm not sure Mladic knew that the battalion had gone until I told ..." [Interpretation] Find this passage. It's the second paragraph on the page, five lines down: [In English] "I'm not sure Mladic knew that the battalion had gone until I told him, in a telephone conversation on 28 August, and that I had decided the mortar round had been fired by his troops. He immediately threatened what he would do to the battalion, and I ended the conversation. I would like to know what happened in his headquarter when he learned they had already left under cover of his order; the thought gave me pleasure at that time. I then turned the UN key, and Admiral 'Snuffie' Smith, the NATO Southern Region commander, turned the NATO key, Smith to Smith, as it was known. Force was finally about to be applied according to a plan." [Interpretation] A long, carefully-planned operation of applying force to the Serbs. The occasion was the shelling at Markale. And you go ahead with it, "Smith to Smith"; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't long in the planning. The -- you can trace this incident, if you like, back to the decisions made in the London Conference, and that's what I'm referring to in the middle of that paragraph. I'm connecting those events, if I remember the rest of -- the earlier part of the discussion in the book. I'm trying to find this bit about you -- yeah, I've got it now, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 369: [In English] "On my part, I would choose the targets that achieve the objectives I had set myself, and as part of my overall plan for the use of force, for in addition to NATO's air power, I also had the artillery and the battle groups of the Rapid Reaction Forces to employ in concert with the air attacks." [Interpretation] Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So were you a warring party that had nothing to do with the UN mandate and our approval, in view of your presence in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had everything to do with the UN mandate. We were in the UN, and I had certain mandates to perform; the continuing delivery of aid and the safe area and exclusion zones, to list them. And the nature of the execution of that mandate, as I've just said, changed after or as a result of the decisions of the London Conference. But we were in the UN, and we were reacting to the circumstances that had been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the London Conference and Plans A and B, we are going to deal with that as this cross-examination continues. However, General, you were rather happy with this use of force, and I have the impression that you were fascinated by General Mladic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fascinated, probably not. Very interested, as the person I was dealing with, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, from time to time, one gains the impression that you're waging a personal war against Mladic, and your soldiers and Mladic's soldiers, and civilians, are getting killed in the process. Actually, not yours; only Mladic's. Did you try to vanquish Mladic during the war?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would want to place on record that I certainly had some soldiers killed, and by Bosnian Serb fire, at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first question, whether you wished to vanquish Mladic, humiliate him, simply win, and did that contribute to our suffering?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't want to humiliate him, and I wasn't interested in increasing the suffering of anybody. What I was faced was a commander, and the burden of what I was required to do and play a part in was to change the intentions of that commander and the -- and those around him, such as yourself. And in that sense, of course it's personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us leave aside the fact that you did not have the right to do that, because we did not allow you to enter our country on that condition. So let us look at this, 369.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You should put your question instead of making statements. I'm telling you this umpteen times. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are objecting, since I'm such an amateur, but I'm going to learn in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please look at the 15th line from the bottom: [In English] "Within three days, the siege of Sarajevo was broken. The third set of targets were those intended to change Mladic's intentions by attacking his personal sense of control. Clearly, the combined effects of the first two categories of targets impacted on his, too. All the bombing was aimed at undermining him as a commander, but I also sought to attack specifically his needs to control. An example of such a target was a military facility in the village where his parents were buried. I was --" Pardon. "... where his parents were buried. It was attacked repeatedly, in the knowledge that in Mladic's culture, a failure to protect the bones of one's ancestors is something of a shameful dereliction of family duty. Matching these attacks, and to increase the pressure, we told the Bosniak press that Mladic could not look after his parents' remains." [Interpretation] General, which mandate allowed you to attack a culture in this way and to inflict such humiliation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the mandate was that that flowed from the security zones -- exclusion zones and the safe areas and the London Conference, and the -- if General Mladic was humiliated, all he had to do was to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, this was sacrilege in relation to things held sacred by him, the graves of his parents. And you informed his opponents, the Bosniak press, that now he couldn't do anything about it. Is that not a personal war, General? Would Mladic have ever done that kind of thing to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think so, if he had the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this a personal war, on your side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, I needed to change -- I understood that I needed to change this commander -- General Mladic's intentions, and explained in the book, is how I was setting out to do it. And I didn't bomb the graveyard. The military target was what was bombed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, I think the witness was turning his microphone on as -- I'm not sure his first words were caught, but maybe they'll be caught on the tape, which I think was "I told you," was the -- I think the first few words he began the sentence with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know I had the microphone off. It's on again now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that at the beginning, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it not clear, on the basis of all of this, that in planned fashion, and quite consciously, you became a wartime ally of our enemy, and that you did not start disciplining the Army of Republika Srpska or punishing it, but simply you tried to change the situation on the ground, at the detriment of the Serbs, in order to make it possible for the Muslims and Croats to have a better negotiating position? Right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not doing anything to improve the -- by my actions, an intention to improve the situation for the other party. Inevitably, what we were doing, attacking the Bosnian Serb Army, would alter that balance. That, I quite agree. But that was not my purpose. My purpose was to reimpose the exclusion zones and to get the weapons withdrawn from them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us now look at the next page, 370, and then we're going to tender all three pages. So it's the same document, next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom: [In English] "With the start of the second phase of the NATO-UN action, the Croatians and the launched a joint offensive towards Banja Luka from the positions gained in South-West Bosnia and the Krajinas in August. They made a rapid progress, aided, no doubt, by the effects of the bombing." [Interpretation] Have you found that part?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It's the bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had its own air force. They got one in you, in NATO. You were meeting those needs of theirs in the war; right? Quite simply, you helped them succeed; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where have I said that in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not in that paragraph, but you'll see another document. Can these three pages be admitted? 1D3192, could we call that up, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, is it correct that you were making whatever they expected come true? In other words --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is "they," and what were they expecting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Muslim Army, they needed this. They needed you to bomb certain targets for their purposes and to make it possible to change the situation on the ground. General, this is a letter sent to you by the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. If you ask a question, you have to wait until you hear the answer from the witness. Do you like to comment on the last statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Needed you to bomb? They may have wanted me to bomb certain targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look -- could you cast a glance at this and look at these targets that were ordered or commissioned by General Delic. Look at them and see how many you actually did hit. This is information provided to you as to which targets should be hit around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can we see the portion of the document or any previous evidence that supports the assertion that these were targets ordered or commissioned by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first sentence: "Please forward the following data to the NATO South Wing Command so that their aircraft could take action against the mentioned targets in the exclusion zone around Sarajevo." And further up, it says "The Republic of Herzegovina," the "General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina," "the 4th of September, 1995," "For UNPROFOR BH Command, attention General Smith." So General Delic is sending you a list of desirable targets so that you could forward those to NATO so that NATO could hit those targets. Have you kept this letter somewhere in your own archives?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it. Is there any evidence that it was received? I mean, it may have been. I don't recall it at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we review the remaining pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The remaining pages -- if we had enough time, General, we would have collated this list with the list of sites that were actually targeted. You will see that what he had asked for was honoured, to a large degree. And then the last question before the break -- or, actually, could this be admitted? General, is it correct that you made an effort to that effect and that, basically, there was no difference between the United Nations and the NATO force? Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- there's a NATO force and a United Nations force, and they were separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, as to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I have a couple of concerns. First of all, I don't see that the witness was able to tell us anything about it. Secondly, there were assertions apparently premised in the document that the witness didn't have an opportunity to answer, because they were overtaken, as is kind of a common practice, by multiple questions, the last one of which was answered. So what we have on the record thus far is assertions about this document by the accused, and little more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document was addressed to General Smith, and you don't remember having received this kind of document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'm not saying it wasn't. It may have been received and nobody did anything with it. I note it isn't signed. The -- it's also on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is an English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to see the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, if the original's got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's not signed in the original, either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then my point is -- stands. The -- what I'm -- the point I was about to make was that the -- this is on the 4th. We've actually -- I'd have to check to be absolutely sure of the chronology, but I think we're at -- we've -- we have been carrying out the -- what came to be called the air/land plan for some three days, if not four days by now, and most of the artillery targets that we attacked, as opposed to reacted to, have been struck by this stage. That's my only comment on it at this stage. Without a map and so forth and a chronology of what was fired at, I couldn't make a further comparison with any accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In light of the fact that this document was addressed to the General, and the General put some context in this document, on that basis we'll admit this. We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1012, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It's time to take a break, Mr. Karadzic, but if --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask whether I could put just one more question so that we would round off this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but I wanted to revisit the one issue which relates to the intercept which we admitted as D1011 being marked for identification. But at the time, it didn't occur to me it was an intercept. It's a conversation between General Mladic and General Smith. So if General Smith could confirm that such conversation took place, we have a basis to admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, such a conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that will be admitted in full. Yes, one last question before the recess -- before the break, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Actually, my question had to do about the unity achieved; namely, that the UN army and the NATO army became one. Can we now have the book again, that is, 1D3196, page 23 in e-court and it is page 372 in the book, itself, and then we would add these pages to what has already been admitted. Please have a look at this, 372, towards the bottom of the page: [In English] "November 2004, the EU took over with the force of 7.000. In truth, it was essentially the same force. When the UN forces became NATO's, most of the troops already on the ground remained, swapping their blue berets for national ones and the UN flag for NATO's. When the EU took over from the NATO, the same troops largely remained once again, swapping their NATO flag to the EU one. We only have one set of forces, which are always double or triple earmarked for all the different organisations and purposes in which they are used."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this part of your book evidence of the fact that you were aware of that? And we saw that you said earlier on that you made every effort for the Rapid Reaction Force to resemble NATO as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is part of my book, and what I'm saying there is what I've just said to you before. We have one group of soldiers. They are differentiated by the organisation they're answering to or -- and are directing their activities and the mission or purpose for which they are being employed, and so you can find the same forces moving between NATO and the UN or, as I describe in the book, the European Union, drawn from the member nations concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That has a different name in our language in the wars that were fought in our part of the world. Those wearing three caps, two are in your pocket, and the third one's on your head, depending on who's in power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Another statement. Given that we have already added page 368 to the exhibit, we'll add pages from 369 until the end, i.e., page 373. Although you didn't refer to page 371, it would be better to admit all the pages -- relevant pages. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Before we break, I just wanted to seek some clarification as we pursue the witness scheduling issues the Court mentioned. The Court indicated, in its oral remarks, that it was minded to continue hearing witnesses until the first week of March, which raises a slight ambiguity I wanted to resolve, whether that meant -- since March 1st falls on Tuesday, whether that meant the end of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Until the 3rd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the 3rd of March, being a Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 65 ter 9903. I'm not sure if we have the English version. Perhaps we can put up only the English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting: General, do you recall that telephone conversation in which General Mladic informed you that he had prohibited all fire on the city? That was the conversation regarding Markale on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall conversations on that day. The specific one when he said he'd prohibited fire, I don't know which one that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at this. Here, the deputy commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Colonel Cedomir Sladoje, is issuing an order and saying, point 1: "I caution again, all the unit commanders, pursuant to my order on restricting fire at the city of Sarajevo without approval from the corps command post. "... by 1400 hours, inform the corps command whether you opened fire between 1000 and 1200 hours at Sarajevo ..." "... if you have inform us -- if you have, notify the target, calibre, weapon," et cetera. Do you know that even before that date when you spoke to Karadzic [as interpreted], all fire upon the city was prohibited?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, and I don't think it was, in that I recall that fire was -- rounds were -- did come into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that was the case only when we were being shot at. Returning fire is legitimate. I'm talking about fire without the approval of the corps command. This says it's prohibited to fire without the approval of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know and I wasn't privy to the correspondence or orders of that corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall that in that conversation, Mladic promised you to investigate the incident?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said he'd investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document, where information is being sought, as part of the investigation, that Mladic had promised?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether that's because of the Mladic promises, I don't know, but I can see the corps commander wishing to gather this information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not clear to me it falls precisely under the guide-lines. But I think sufficient context has been provided, so I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1013, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3177 in e-court, preferably in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you now kindly look at a short summary of this crisis, penned by a very renowned doyen of journalism, David Binder. It says: "Amid the roar and blinding flashes of NATO's air-strikes against the Bosnian Serbs, the impetus for the bombing was obscured. The August 28 explosion is in a narrow, enclosed market in the centre of Sarajevo that killed 37 people. Within a day of that explosion, investigators for the UN Protection Force, under Lieutenant-General Rupert Smith, concluded beyond all reasonable doubt that the lethal mortar round had been fired from a Bosnian Serb position in the suburb of Lukavica, one and a half to three and a half kilometres south-west of the market-place. On August 30, NATO's bombs began to fall. "The crucial UN report on the market massacre is classified secret, but four specialists - a Russian, a Canadian and two Americans - have raised serious doubts about its conclusion, suggesting instead that the mortar was fired not by the Serbs, but by the Bosnian government forces." [Interpretation] Were you aware that in addition to that Russian deputy commander of the Sarajevo Sector, there were also one Canadian and two Americans who doubted the investigation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you aware that this UN report was classified secret?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to go and look at it, but no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now look at the next paragraph: "Similar suspicions were raised following the February 5, 1994, mortar shell explosion that killed 68 Sarajevans in the adjacent Markale market-place. The origin of that shell was never determined officially. The UN's after-action report in 1994 (also classified secret) was based on separate examinations of the impact site by 11 artillery specialists over a period of 9 days and ran 46 pages. General Smith's report was based on three hours of on-the-spot investigation and covered only one page." And a bit further below, Colonel Demurenko is mentioned: "On August 29, Demurenko announced that the probability of hitting a street less than 30 feet wide from one or two miles away, the distance to the nearest Serb artillery positions, was one to one million." Are you aware of and did anyone agree with this conclusion that the probability of this round being fired from Serbian positions was one to a million?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear precisely what's being measured here, but the civilian areas of Sarajevo was a substantial target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a general statement, and like all general statements, they are rejected by the Defence. Let's talk about a specific incident: Markale, 28th August. Did you agree, did the United Nations agree, or anyone else -- did anyone else agree with the claim made by Colonel Demurenko that the possibility of hitting a nine-metre-wide street - I think 30 feet is about nine metres, right? - is one to a million?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The General answered that he didn't know what measures were taken at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Were the United Nations aware of this estimate that the probability of making this shot was one to a million? That's all.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, and it was me who had to be aware of it, that this was brought to my attention. And, as I've said, I don't understand why it should have been, since the civilian areas of Sarajevo were a much greater area than nine-metre wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, you concluded beyond a reasonable doubt that the Serbs fired that round, and that also implies an intention to hit that place crawling with civilians. That estimate, one to a million, probably refers to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let's see another document, 1D3119. We can remove this one for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1D3191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I just have to question the logic behind your last question. The fact that a mortar round lands in a particular place, and is fired from a particular direction, may give rise to an assessment of where it came from, but it doesn't necessarily imply an intention to hit that exact spot. We've already heard testimony, in respect of mortar fire, that the -- as it were, the circle of error with a mortar round, even firing two mortar bombs from the same tube one after the other, can be considerable. So for my part, I find that question a non sequitur.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. But the point is that I'm charged with intentional fire at a group of civilians on the market-place. That's one. And, second, these experts say that the possibility of hitting that specific street deliberately is one to a million. Let us now look at this telegram sent by General Janvier. It's an authorisation for NATO action: [In English] "... hope that when taken with our Z-1535 and Z-1537 on the 29th of August, and our Z-1560, dated 1 September 1995, you will have enough information to answer any further technical questions on the matter." [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, then. Under 1, it says: [In English] "The American journalist who rang "Tanjug" quotes Colonel Andrei Demurenko, Chief of Staff Sector Sarajevo Headquarter, as having reportedly told TASS that hitting a nine-metre-wide street from a distance of three to four kilometres would be a million to one chance. There is no disagreement about the difficulty of deliberately hitting such a target. It is, however, most likely that the shot was just fired -- be fired from the general area. That it landed in the market square was a great misfortune that bear [sic] the odds." [Interpretation] And then below, in the second paragraph, towards the middle: [In English] "The point that any fire from far out would be blind fire is agreed; as explained in the above paragraph, it is not believed that the shot was aimed specifically at the market-place."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a telegram from General Janvier that confirms that it is unlikely that this was deliberate fire on this place, but I put it to you that it could not have been fired from the Serbian side at all, and I'm going to try to prove that. Were you aware of this opinion of General Janvier's?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall ever having seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1014, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to 1D3177, please. It's David Binder's report. Page 2. It says: "The Canadian specialist, an officer with extensive service in Bosnia, said, in a telephone interview, that the UN report, which he'd seen, was highly suspect. He cited anomalies with the fuse of the mortar shell recovered from the market-place crater. Unlike the fuses of four other shells that hit Sarajevo that morning, this one, he said, had not come from a mortar tube at all. He added that he and fellow Canadian officers in Bosnia were convinced that the Muslim government dropped both the 5th February and the 28th August mortar shells on the Sarajevo markets. "A US administration official who may not be identified further says, 'It is impossible to see the street level of the market-place from the distance and location of the Serb gun positions.'" Is this correct? Do you know that this street was not in the field of vision of any Serb position?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, says this American official: "A projectile fired from such a distance would have a high trajectory. But since the characteristic whizzing sound could not be heard, the shell could not have fallen from a great height." He also says: "The trajectory of the shell was rather low, which indicates a range of several hundred yards." That is to say, Bosnian government positions, or: "... perhaps this modified mortar shell was dropped from somewhere in town or thrown into the market-place from someplace in the vicinity." Have you ever heard any of these opinions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which ones you're -- of the list you've -- do you want me to comment on all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll finish to see the summing up by Mr. Binder: "The UN command in Sarajevo has offered a point-by-point rebuttal to these arguments. Curiously, it agrees with the dissenters on three basic points --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it is not the time to read out this clipping. What is your question to the General?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question is contained here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you agree that the shell had a low trajectory? Did you agree that if it had been a Serbian shot, the probability was one to a million, and, thirdly, that whoever was shooting was shooting blind? All these things indicate that it is unlikely to have come from Serb positions. Do you agree with this statement made by the UN, based on this telegram by General Janvier, who confirmed this a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. My quick read of the beginning of that document that you refer me to gives me no indication that the UN have said any of those things in the way you have put them in that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's contained in the telegram by General Janvier. Do you want me to put it back on the screen? Can I have that document back, please, 1D -- no, it's D1014. D1014. I'll read it to you while we're waiting. In the first paragraph, it says --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the screen. It can be -- I've read the front. We can go to the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't have it on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't either. Yes, now it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, it says the odds are a million to one. Then in the middle of the second paragraph: [In English] "The point that any fire from far out would be blind fire is agreed." [Interpretation] "The point that any fire from far out would be blind fire is agreed." So it's agreed that it would be blind fire. And then --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is the word "blind fire"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the middle of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It begins with the words: "The point ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was still on the first paragraph numbered 1. Okay, he writes there "blind fire." It did not aim specifically at the market-place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "It should also be pointed out that the Yugoslav mortars fire at a higher trajectory at a shorter range." This is a matter for ballistics experts, but you do see, don't you, that the United Nations took this into account, your subordinate commander agreed, and the United Nations agreed on certain points?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that he is saying that there, and this is all second-guessing the decision that had already been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was from the 31st of August. This is only proving that the decision was made too hastily. Your own commander seems to be saying that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where he says I made a hasty decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you are saying that by saying the decision had already been reached, for better or worse. You made your decisions several days before, and on the 31st your subordinate commander is making certain points and reservations and expressing doubt about the conclusions. It's not the telegram that is wrong, it's the decision that was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it just seems to me, to be fair to the witness, since we're running back and forth between two documents, I don't see "reservations" in the document attributed to Janvier, and the effort that's being made here is to try to link the factors or the reservations expressed in the Binder article to some parallel facts discussed in the Janvier report. But if Dr. Karadzic wants to confront the witness about alleged reservations expressed by Janvier in that -- in the document he wrote, then he should point those out, rather than build them as an assumption to the question when the witness is being bounced back and forth between two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Since I believe the General would be capable of dealing with this question, I'll ask him to proceed to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not quite clear if I've got a question outstanding or not at this stage. No, I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His question seems to be the one that General Janvier was expressing his reservation and alluding to the effect that your decision was wrong. So what is your comment to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't see where he is saying he is disagreeing with me. The point I was trying to make earlier, I think, has just been made by the -- Mr. Tieger. You've -- this is all after my decision, and it's my commander, as it were, producing arguments contrary to those such as you raised from the article by this man, Binder, which is published a whole month later. They are not actually -- Binder's article is -- is something that's much later than the questions that General Janvier is attempting to provide answers for in -- or comments that he's effectively trying to answer in this paper.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the distinguished Mr. Tieger doubts the fact that this is Janvier's, then we can have the first page displayed again. 1D3177, perhaps we could go back to that document now. Page 2. The second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another US administration official, who may not be identified, says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note : We have not found that particular section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then it says that the command accepts these three matters contained in the telegram of General Janvier's. And then Binder says: "Why would the Bosnian government be killing its own people? It is a fact that a week before the massacre in the market-place, the government forces launched a fierce attack against Vogosca --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The page has just been displayed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, with that speed, the interpreters cannot catch up with you. So indicate the page and read slow. And we can all read this document. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that this offensive had started around mid-August -- or, rather, after the 20th of August? A week before this incident, there was this strong Muslim offensive?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember that there were some actions around Gorazde in the August time. And if I recall it correctly -- yes, if I recall it correctly, the judgement was that they -- this was fighting along the front-line and that the essential element -- the civil element of the safe area was not threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean the Serb civilians that were targeted by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the action around Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And now the second paragraph from the bottom, for the interpreters and the other participants: [In English] "Then the ambassador -- the assistant secretary, Richard Holbrooke, went --" [Interpretation] "... went to the Balkans to push President Clinton's peace plan. Only a pretext was needed. It is clear that the air-strikes had already been planned before Holbrooke went to the Balkans to push the peace plan." So: "Only a pretext was needed." Targets were bombed only 39 hours after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should have the next page. And now the last paragraph: "Once the bombing was underway, General Rasim Delic, commander of Bosnian forces in Sarajevo, began picking targets - phoning Admiral W.A. Owens, vice-chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, daily with his wish list of sites. The Pentagon then passed these on to NATO in Naples. As one US officer put it, 'We have become the Muslim Air Force.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There you are, General. This is how this renowned US journalist sees this entire action, and I'm sure that he has excellent sources. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard of this Mr. Binder before, so -- and if I have, I've never kept his name in my memory. And I'm not aware that he'd written this article on the 2nd of October, some month after the events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very well-known journalist, very highly regarded, but all right, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can go to the witness stand and give evidence. Refrain from making statements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that we are going to be able to deal with everything through other witnesses, so there will be no need for me to testify. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any basis, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an analysis of a respectable journalist regarding the crisis that this witness spoke about. It's a question of context, and it provides a thorough review of what was going on, actually. And worldwide, there was this suspicion with regard to the interpretation that had been provided for this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By now, you should be familiar with the Chamber's practice. We do not admit a third party's news clipping. You can call Mr. Binder or Mr. Demurenko or the Canadian officer or US officer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll probably do that. Can we have 1D408, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say, General, that you did not target civilian targets during that campaign; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what we have now, a report of the War Presidency of the Municipality of Stari Grad up to the 31st of August. Could we scroll down a bit, and let's look at the penultimate paragraph. I am being informed here, as the president of the republic, about what was going on: "On the 30th of August, 1995, NATO forces bombed our positions, settlements and roads and caused significant material damage, and three civilians were injured on that occasion." General, sir, settlements, as in neighbourhoods, and roads, are they civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very probably. There were civilian buildings and so forth there. I don't know -- you'd need to give me the grid references and so forth, and I'd need a list of where we attacked to tell you whether or not we thought there was a military target there. I am confident that in each case that we attacked the targets, particularly on that opening stage of the campaign, that we had made great care that, A, that there was a military target there, and that there was the very least possibility of damage to civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before continuing with this line of questions, could you help us -- help me as regards how this is relevant to your case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this witness and many other witnesses, in their very general statements, say that it was Serbs who were firing at Sarajevo, disregarding the fact that Sarajevo was full of legitimate military objectives, brimming with such targets, and we are going to prove that. If we show the next page -- or, rather, the last page, we are going to show that the Rapid Deployment Force was firing and that civilians were getting killed. The core of the matter is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. Yes. Are you in the course of answering my question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. I am trying to say that it is legitimate to question the credibility of this witness to show that he was an interested party, a warring party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is to be found relevant, it is only marginally relevant. I'll allow you to continue on this question, but conclude this part very briefly, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm going to abandon this topic, but let us just have a look at this last page to see that civilians were getting killed as well and that Hresa and Biosko were two neighbourhoods that were bombed, and that apartment buildings were damaged, and that two children were wounded, livestock were killed, and so on. First of all, let us see what all of this looks like. And, secondly, from the next topic, you will see what General Mladic's thinking is with regard to this crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you see that civilian neighbourhoods were being bombed, General, Gradiste, Bulozi, Hresa and Biosko were bombed as well. Nikola Kosmajac, you see his name and surname, a civilian, he was killed in that attack, and four other civilians, two of whom were children, were wounded, and a great deal of damage was inflicted. Is that what is written here?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is written there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is a report sent to the president of the republic. It's not a media thing of any sort. It is a report sent by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't think, in this case, the witness has provided any illumination on this. And also, at the moment, I want to see the original, which I haven't had a chance to see in full yet. So at the moment, I object.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the Serbian version? The Serbian version is in e-court. Here it is. The first page -- sorry, it has a number and a date. Can we have page 2 now. Here it is, a seal and a signature. And can we see the third page. That is an appendix, because the bombing took place after the report was written. This is the addendum, where it says exactly what happened. This is an absolutely authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would that change your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we have a signed document in Cyrillic. Then we have an undated, unsigned supplemental -- so-called supplemental report in different type-set and in Latin. And so it does not change my objection; it underscores it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness did not say anything about this document, so we will not admit this. You will have another opportunity to tender that through another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness doesn't have to say anything. It was his soldiers who did this, under his command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's not something -- I don't want to be on my feet during -- any more than necessary during the course of these proceedings. And very often, of course, the commentary is injected well before I can rise, but it is a recurring pattern. It is not a reflection of Mr. Karadzic's experience or lack of experience in the courtroom. He knows very well the prohibition and the nature of the commentary, and willfully persists on doing so. And I want to note that it happens far more frequently than anyone is really in a position to explicitly note in the record or object to. Otherwise, we'd be on -- I'd be on my feet all the time and the Court would be making admonitions much more often than it already is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Karadzic, what you've got to remember is that interjections by you are not only ill placed, they have absolutely no evidential value whatsoever unless they are in the form of a question. And as I've said to you before, a question isn't evidence. It's the answer to the question that's evidence. If a witness adopts what you say or agrees with what you say, all well and good, but otherwise it's simply the independent evidence of the witness that counts. So you complain about not having enough time on some occasions. If you waste it by interjections and comments, then you only have yourself to blame.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But with all due respect, I had a good look at this, and I saw how one of the Prosecutors was examining during the Milosevic case, and I learned that from him. If necessary, I'll give you the name. Could I have 1D3160. Actually, it's Mr. Nice, who was very creative in that regard, and I thought that I could treat witnesses that way, witnesses of the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unacceptable, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, yes. First of all, that's an unacceptable comparison, and, in any event, it's a useless comparison. What a Prosecutor may or may not have done in another case has no bearing upon your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3160, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- actually, no, this is not you. This is an unidentified speaker, an unidentified speaker. The identified speaker is General Mladic. And now we could move on to the second page to see what it was that General Mladic was saying at the time about the very same things.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go back? I think you've got two unidentified speakers there. I saw a "C" and a "D." Which one am I paying attention to? Oh, I see, it's a second call, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's a different person.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. So it's "D" you want me to pay attention to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "C" is some intermediary, someone who made sure that the connection was there. Here, Mladic says: "Well, from 200 hours last night until now, they have been attacking. They have attacked a number of positions in Republika Srpska, both military and civilian." And further on, it says: "They also attacked civilian targets, especially in the sector of Sarajevo, Hadzici, Vogosca, and so on. There are several hundred people wounded and killed." And also he says further on: "They attacked everything around, and it's not important now if they attack this and that. I don't want to go into details. They attacked everything. Material damage is enormous, and there are many casualties, both soldiers and civilians." Further on, he says: "Yes, yes, particularly in Blazuj, because there they started attacking with artillery the day before yesterday, and they hit a church in which 47 people were wounded and one person was killed." And then he says: "On Assumption Day." That is a big holiday, a big Serbian -- or, rather, a big Christian holiday. And then Mladic says: "Yes, yes, even some schools were hit." And all sorts of things happened on that day. Could we see the next page. You see: "Mladic: We did not fire a shell, and there is not a single shell that could kill hundreds of people, even if they were all in a barrel." Perhaps it's the previous page in English, actually. Oh, yes, it's toward the bottom of the page: "Firstly, we did not fire the shell, and, secondly, no mortar shell can hurt over 100 people, even if they had all been in some big barrel. It is absolutely clear that this is their media trick, just like Markale I." You see, in a private conversation, in the absence of the public, General Mladic is fully convinced of what he is saying; that so many people could not have been killed by a single shell and that this was designed in the same way that Markale I was.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date of this document, which would be interesting to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Around the 4th or 5th of September. We're going to see that from another document. At any rate, during the bombing, from the beginning of the bombing onwards, because he says they are still bombing.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't tell me that Mladic is convinced of it at all. If it tells me anything, he's trying to convince Unidentified Speaker D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a private telephone conversation. It is not intended for the public. He is speaking to a friend of his, obviously, and he is assuring the friend that that was not the case. Now, we are talking now about Mladic's state of mind, about Mladic's genuine belief and position. This is an intercept, just as we admitted another intercept along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how do we know this is a private telephone conversation between friends?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it has the same status like the intercept with Krajisnik, Excellency. This man is talking as well, but, at any rate, it's not an official conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You ask a question instead of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I was also going to note, in addition to the general area that you alluded to, that Mr. Karadzic did ask a question, General Smith answered the question, and now Mr. Karadzic is engaged in arguing with him about that answer. His question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: True, I agree with you. Proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just the last part: "Well, they did it at Markale again, because Markale is well known, and we really have nothing to do with it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I'm not asking you to say whether you had heard this conversation before. I'm asking you whether this is consistent with what Mladic was saying to you; namely, that the Serb side was not responsible for what happened then.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had said that to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, we see no basis to admit this intercept through General Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a moment ago we admitted a very similar document, an intercept with Krajisnik. I am talking about admissibility. Krajisnik is talking to an unidentified speaker again. The witness confirmed that this is consistent, that Mladic had said the same thing to him. We are showing that Mladic was saying this to people off the record. This confirms Mladic's conviction that that is what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number of the Krajisnik intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's P2272 and also P2271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I know you want to deliberate, but if I could make a couple of quick points before you do. To refresh your recollection about the Krajisnik intercept, it -- making the comparison between the two and pointing to the fact that they both may have involved an interlocutor who was not an official is an irrelevancy. In the Krajisnik intercept, we see Mr. Krajisnik, a close confidant of the accused, a leading member of the Bosnian Serb leadership, talking about the Bosnian Serb leadership position on hostages and the uses to which the threats against those people would be made, so it's a direct expression of that. This intercept, Dr. Karadzic tried to get some acquiescence from the witness that this is a reflection of General Mladic's true conviction. The witness said, I don't see that at all, it looks like he's trying to convince someone else. And, in fact, in a portion of the intercept that Mr. Karadzic failed to put to the witness, and that's at page 15, you see the -- you see General Mladic saying: "Do the best you can to inform the world through our influential people." In other words, again, just as the witness surmised, trying to persuade the interlocutor to do something on the basis of alleged information that Mladic was providing him. Those are two quite different circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to add, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If I can just add that, if you look at the transcript, I believe General Smith said this is consistent with what General Mladic had said to him. You admitted a lot of evidence along those lines during this trial, if it's consistent with the position, so I think this is an easy call for you and it falls squarely within your guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We tend to agree with Mr. Robinson's observation. The witness confirmed that part of Mladic's word were consistent with what he heard, so on that basis we'll admit this. But we mark it for identification, following our usual practice.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1015, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3159 is the next document I would like to ask for. This is a conversation between General Mladic and General Perisic. It is very important that you see, General, what kind of relationship they have and the exchange they have about this incident. Perisic is finished. Now a professor has come. That's towards the bottom. We have to show the bottom of the page. Mladic says: "So all this media scene at Markale," and that's the pretext they found --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter hasn't found this in the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. Mladic says: "They are bombing and imposing a solution by force."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, that it is this bombing campaign that imposed a solution? It is the bombing campaign that led to the peace conference, that was its purpose, and that's how it was planned, as we will show tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. The bombing did not impose a solution. The peace process with -- led by the late Richard Holbrooke, was underway before the end of August. And as you've read my book, you will know there is a period, at the very early stages of the bombing, when Richard Holbrooke is denying its connection with what he is doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times did you speak to Mr. Holbrooke on 28th and 29th August?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I only spoke to him once, but it may have been twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 28th or the 29th?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think probably the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that tomorrow. Let's see what Mladic says here: "Well, connect this. They have no reason to bomb us. They are bombing targets that are 200 kilometres away from Markale, Professor." And then he goes on to say there are no heavy weapons involved: "We are not in a conflict with them. Let them withdraw their heavy weapons." We can now go back to page 1, where Perisic is unable to help him. He says: "I can only wish you good luck with it." And there's nothing else he can do. And then with the professor, Mladic repeats what he said before; that it was a completely staged incident in Markale I as in Markale II. Is that consistent with what the Serbian collocutors, including Mladic, told you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see what you've just pointed to me on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's finish with page 1. Mladic says they are bombing centres, and Mladic -- in English, it's the next page.
