Oh, no, on this page, for instance, Perisic says -- all right, that's gone. Mladic says: "Well, brother, help ..." And so on. And Perisic -- no, that's not here. Can we see the next page. So it's all based on this media orchestration at Markale, and this is their direct pretext and justification to bomb and impose a solution by force. And he's telling this professor they are bombing targets 200 kilometres away from Markale. Is this consistent with what the Serbian side told you all the time about this crisis?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought we were looking at the Perisic-Mladic conversation, but we're now -- we've got another "Unknown" on the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see what this unknown collocutor -- who this unknown collocutor is. Some sort of professor. Is what Mladic is telling this professor consistent with the general Serb position as presented to you during that crisis? Our position was that this was orchestrated by the Muslim side, to bring about the bombing and impose a solution by force.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I had another conversation with General Mladic than the last one of those three that we've already discussed. I think it's the 29th of -- takes place on the 29th of August. I don't think I had another conversation with Mladic since then, so I can't tell you if that's what he thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the Serbian side did tell you they believed it was orchestrated by the Muslim side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Mladic told me, that he suggested that this was -- that the Bosnians had fired this mortar round, themselves, at their own people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted on the same basis, marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is different from the previous intercept. The witness was not able to confirm anything about the content of this document. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. We'll try to -- we'll try to have it admitted through another witness. Can we now see 1D3173. Only the English version should be on the screen, and I will quote from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a letter where the Eastern Bosnia Corps Command informs they had received a copy of a letter sent by General Mladic to General Janvier on the 5th of September. Sorry, the 4th of September is the date of Mladic's letter, this letter, wherein the Eastern Bosnia Corps Command is sharing certain information with its own officers, and they quote a letter from General Mladic to General Janvier, dated 4th September. It says they are dealing again -- it regards, again, Markale I and Markale II, and it says the public is not informed of all sorts of manipulations about Markale I. And on page 3, we can see the most important points made in this letter, and this document will be the last in this series on this subject. In English, it could be page 4. Towards the bottom of the next -- of the page, it says: "Contrary to the provisions of --" Could we see the previous page, just the bottom of the page. That's where the beginning of this sentence is. It says: "Contrary to --" Can you see that? "Contrary to the provisions of this convention --" "In the Sarajevo safe area, contrary to the provisions of this convention, in addition to civilian population, the United Nations also protect part of the units of the 1st Muslim Corps, which is ..." Next page, please. [In English] "... organising eight brigades ..." [Interpretation] And so on. May I ask everyone to look at this paragraph. It indicates also the fire-power of these brigades. Were you aware of these brigades and their fire-power located in the heart of Sarajevo, in the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it went very faint in the thing. I think -- just let me read. Can I ask a bit more about this letter? I'm not clear. I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's show the last page of this letter. It was written by General Mladic. The previous page. And shall we show the first page. The Eastern Bosnia Corps was copied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Got you, right. Now I understand. And your question was: Was I aware of all -- no, I'm not aware of this letter or of that list that -- in those what looked like two paragraphs you had up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of those eight brigades, numbering about 20.000 soldiers, and this fire-power in the heart of the city? Did your people inform you of all the assets in the possession of the Bosnian Army in the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed of what we thought both yourselves and the Bosnian Army had, and I don't recognise that list at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at paragraph 2, the second paragraph, where General Mladic explains to General Janvier what is located in the Serbian part of Sarajevo, around that zone, and how many brigades are facing -- are confronting Serbian Sarajevo from outside the city. There are eight brigades confronting them from within the city and eighteen brigades -- eighteen Muslim brigades, three Croatian brigades, and six independent battalions outside the city, also facing the Serbian part of Sarajevo. Were you aware that the Serbian part of Sarajevo was sandwiched between all these forces gathered from all the areas of Bosnia; Tuzla, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not sandwiched.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I have to show you a map, General, to see if you could agree. But please look at the two paragraphs below this one while I find the map. You see, in the third paragraph, that General Mladic is informing you about 342 heavy weapons of various calibres, 25.000 -- that is to say, 35.000 Muslim soldiers with 865 heavy weapons, et cetera, in the ring around Sarajevo. Did you know that the Muslim army had all this fire-power and manpower?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I say, I do not recognise this -- these numbers or that number of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Shouldn't you be able to recognise them, General, because you were supposed to oversee the other side too?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I don't think they're correct, then how can I possibly recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 65 ter 13636. 65 ter 13636. Can this letter by General Mladic to Janvier be admitted? And can we see just one more page, the last page, where he proposes that a joint expert commission be established. The last paragraph on the last page. He proposes that a joint expert commission be established urgently to investigate into Markale II and the special ammunition used by NATO Rapid Reaction Forces, with toxic and radioactive characteristics, the consequences of which are well known to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that the NATO Rapid Reaction Force used toxic and radioactive ammunition?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Rapid Reaction Force under my command was not using radioactive ammunition, and I don't see how you can have a piece of ammunition as toxic. You don't eat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the bombs that were dropped on Hadzici and other neighbourhoods, did they contain depleted uranium?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt -- I doubt it, and that you would have to ask an air force -- a NATO officer -- I'm sorry, a NATO Air Force officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any artillery outside your control and outside your command in that area? Were there any national contingents outside of your control, contingents that you did not trust and were unable to control, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the artillery group of the Rapid Reaction Force was under my command.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this letter be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1016, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 13636, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this map, and does this show the 20-kilometre total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to see the scale. Yes, okay. Yes, that's approximately 20 kilometres, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, on the one hand, is confronting the 1st Corps inside the city, and, on the other hand, it is bordering territory controlled by Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that our artillery pieces in this zone were unable to fire, whereas the artillery of the Muslims and Croats in that area were trained at us, and they were able to fire because they were not controlled by you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question at all. Your artillery was firing, and firing into Sarajevo. And you asked me about a sandwich, and I can't see how the Bosnian Serb forces are in a sandwich at all. It's Sarajevo that's in the sandwich.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you follow the blue line, General. Do you agree that the blue line is the Muslim combat line, the whole length of the front, and aren't we encircled in this north-west part? We are semi-encircled, like the inner part of Sarajevo is also semi-encircled?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not encircled. You've got plenty of space to your east.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Is this map in evidence? It is. Just one more question before the break. 1D3229, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the Drina Corps Command. The date is 14 September 1995. It explains that the president of Republika Srpska and Richard Holbrooke, the US Deputy Secretary of State and also representative of the US Contact Group, in the peace talks, reached a framework agreement on cessation of hostilities inside the Sarajevo zone and cessation of the NATO bombardment of Republika Srpska. And, point by point: "Both parties to the conflict shall cease all operations within and around the zone of exclusion of heavy weapons in the Sarajevo area." Can we lower the page, please. Point 4: "In the total exclusion zone --" And we need the next page in English: "All heavy weapons of the Muslim Army whose calibre exceeds 82 millimetres for mortars and 100 millimetres for artillery, and all tanks in the zone of exclusion around Sarajevo, shall be placed under the control of UNPROFOR." Do you agree that it was only then, at that time, that the objective was reached, the objective of giving the same treatment to the Muslim side that the Serb side enjoyed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That implies -- I don't really understand your question again. Let me -- let me read it: "Do you agree that it was only then, at that time, that the objective was reached ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it was not interpreted very well. My theory is that it was only then, after the bombardment and after my agreement with Holbrooke that everything should cease, it was only then that the decision was made to control Muslim weapons, too, in that area, in that zone; that the total exclusion zone should apply to them as well, but not in a make -believe way, but in a real way, that Muslim weapons should also be placed under control.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that. There was a weapons collection point -- there was at least one inside Sarajevo, and, to the best of my memory, the weapons that were in there stayed in there throughout this period of -- of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, have you seen the consumption, thousands of shells that were fired at us from Sarajevo city and other thousands that were fired at us from Central Bosnia? These shells which were falling on us and were fired from the city of Sarajevo were from the total exclusion zone. Mladic mentions 342 artillery pieces, and these artillery pieces have not been placed under control, General; correct? How could they have fired? Did they fire at us with your approval or did they fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Make your questions simpler. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a mix of commentary and a string of questions, to which -- apparently designed as rhetorical questions to which the accused is seeking no answer, and they serve, therefore, as commentary. So as the Court noted, if he wants to put questions, he needs to do so in an understandable way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is simple, General. Did the Muslims use their heavy artillery pieces and fire at us from the centre of the city with your approval or were they firing from weapons which were outside of your control?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not fire with my approval.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's probably the time for the break. Could this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to leave that in the Court's hands, Your Honour. I don't -- I don't see a great deal of illumination. On the other hand, I don't have a strong objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1017, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 3.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D3185.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we are coming back to the early days of your mandate and your stay with us. This is a letter which you and your associate, Enrique Aguilar, wrote to Professor Koljevic on the 4th of February. You were asked on the first day, General, about convoys and these humanitarian issues. Do you know who, among us, was charged with the convoy issues and humanitarian issues?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, although I seem -- I mean, I'm prompted by this letter to -- that our point of contact was the -- Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will it remind you if I tell you that Vice-President Koljevic, who is a Shakespearean scholar and a renowned university professor, was the president of our Committee for Co-operation with United Nations, which was also in charge of humanitarian issues? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you reminded me. Yup.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that a president cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you scroll down? Can you scroll down a bit further to see Professor Koljevic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is a high level, that a vice-president should be the chairman to the Committee for Co-operation with United Nations, that is to say, the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's a senior person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 4th of February, it seems that your stay was marked by good understanding and co-operation with the Serbian side, both the civilian and the military structures. Does this document testify to that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It testifies that we communicated our intentions. I don't know that it -- you know, what happened next. I don't know what the result of this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember that this document also concerns the civilian use of the airport for both sides? Ilidza-Lukavica, this is where the Serbs would pass, and Butmir-Dobrinja is the route along which the Muslims would pass along? Is that what this document envisages?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly refers to those routes and the times people would travel on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, General, that in that case, civilians did not have to use the tunnel at all, because for the civilians from both sides, it was possible to cross across the airport during two hours in the morning and in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why that precludes them using the tunnel. They had an alternative, that's all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1018, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D3161.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General Mladic writes to you on the 11th of February. He's responding to your letter dated the 10th of February. Can you please have a look at this. He says, in the middle of the first paragraph: "In our letter number 06/17-40 of 17th of January 1995, we informed General Rose of the Muslim force's offensive activities in this area ..." [In English] "... by which they flagrantly violate the agreement on cessation of hostilities signed on 31st of December, 1992." [Interpretation] Further on, he informs you that they are carrying out offensive activities in a continuous manner against Fikret Abdic, which is another Muslim faction that we were on good terms with, on the entire territory of the Bihac pocket. And, finally: [In English] "I am convinced that the unconditional withdrawal of the Muslim forces to the lines of 31st of December, 1994, would contribute to the peace and stability in the region. Therefore, I expect you to become engaged in this matter in order to calm down the conflict between the forces under Fikret Abdic's and Alija Izetbegovic's command." [Interpretation] Do you remember this letter, and isn't it somewhat strange for Western stereotypes that a Serbian general is trying to calm down an inter-Muslim conflict?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's telling me to calm it down, while he will endeavour to remain neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. He cannot become involved in this, but he wants the inter-Muslim conflict to calm down so that the cessation of hostilities would work. Do you remember this letter, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the letter, specifically, but I certainly remember the incident he's referring to or the incidents he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we scroll down a bit -- could we please do that? No, the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see "Sarajevo HQ, crypto," so it was received there; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, and I'm sure it was, but I -- I just don't remember the letter, itself, very clearly, while I remember the circumstances that are referred to in it. Indeed, I've signed it, so there's my initials there, on the 12th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1019, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 1D3186. We can have the translation on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Two days later, General Mladic is writing to General Smith, and he says: "Mr. General, the Muslim forces from the area of Bihac have again launched a fierce offensive in the direction of Ripac, Skocaj and Medjudrazje, south of Bihac." That means the Serbian territories: "For the third day running, they have brutally and indiscriminately destroyed Serbian towns and villages using all the weapons that are available to them. They loot and torch the houses ..." And so on and so forth. The following paragraph: "Since the signing of the agreement on the cessation of hostilities, this has been the second major Muslim offensive from the so-called Bihac protected zone." Further on, it says that: "It is indicative that this offensive, too, was undertaken ahead of the scheduled meeting of the commanders of the warring parties which is to be held on the 15th February 1995 ..." Were you aware of this abuse of the Bihac protected zone which was used in this manner by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I can remember this -- the fighting taking place there, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D1020.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 1D3216.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D3216, please help me to identify this. It's NorlogBat, BH Command, UNPROFOR, the 12th of February, 1995. Could we please have a look at the next page. It's a daily sitrep. We can see it here, "General Overview," and then five or six lines down it says: [In English] "Friday night, an aircraft was observed flying at low altitude over the area east of Tuzla, with every indication that it was going to land. It was assumed that this would happen in Tuzla East, where there is an extended highway strip. The UN APCs which were sent out to investigate the matter were prevented by the BiH Army from doing so. It therefore cannot be confirmed whether the aircraft actually landed or not or whether a load was dropped at low altitude." [Interpretation] Do you remember that at the time, a resolution on a no-fly zone was in force?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a no-fly zone, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this UN sitrep talk about the violation of the no-fly zone in Tuzla, which was a territory under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It describes an aeroplane flying low, at a low altitude. I don't think anyone's established whether it's -- at that stage, whether it was a cleared flight or not, since the no-fly zone was conducted by the NATO authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But is it obvious that the Muslim army prevented the UNPROFOR from checking this and that --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. It says it there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection to this document. But in other circumstances, I may well raise the lack of utility in asking a witness simply to confirm that that's what a document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given your position and given the context, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1021, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please see 1D3162.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 14th of February, 1995, and it says: "To the UNPROFOR Command, Sector North-East," and so on. Can we please have a look at the next page now. This telegram is forwarded. You are sending a letter of General Mladic, addressed to General Smith, which says in the first paragraph: [In English] "We are gravely concerned over the frequent use of Tuzla Airport by the Muslim side. The aircraft are bringing weapons, ammunition and war material for their needs." [Interpretation] And further on, it says: [In English] "Unfortunately, this pirate activity of their aircraft is enabled by the NATO air force, and the Muslim army does not allow your force to control the loads." [Interpretation] And further on it says: [In English] "I ask you to take urgent measures to stop these peace-threatening activities. Otherwise, we will be compelled to take the necessary measures regarding the Muslim side's violation of the Tuzla safe area, which is, in the presence of your forces, turning into a war base for Islamic countries." [Interpretation] Do you remember this crisis, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the incidents, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1022, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 1D3163.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also correspondence between you and General Mladic, who is writing to you on the 24th of February and says -- the letter is addressed to the attention of -- he's writing to the command in Zagreb, but it's also forwarded to you and General De Lapresle. And it says that: "On the 23rd of February, 1995, at about 2010 hours, a transport plane, with weapons and military equipment, landed again at Tuzla Airport's secondary runway. It was escorted by two NATO fighter aircraft ..." In the second paragraph, it says that: "... the NATO and UNPROFOR forces ..." [In English] "... were there and at Tuzla airport itself." [Interpretation] So they were there: [In English] "Those forces are doing nothing to prevent the violation of the relevant UN Security Council resolution prohibiting the import of weapons and military equipment. "General, you have accepted the obligation to control the airspace over former BH, and you are very eager, both verbally and practically, to do so with regard to the Serb side." [Interpretation] Do you remember this protest?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that two resolutions were violated here, the resolution prohibiting the importation of weapons and the resolution prohibiting flights?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't know what came in on those aeroplanes. I will agree with you that there was every indication from our own reporting on the ground that an aeroplane on occasions had landed at one of the alternative airstrips in the vicinity of Tuzla. We never, in UNPROFOR, got to the bottom of it as to just who was responsible and how they were avoiding the NATO no-fly zone measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please have a look at the paragraph beginning with: "Although we try not to --" [In English] " ... regard this situation as an example of open partiality towards our enemies, it is difficult to avoid such an impression. Our suspicions, that senior UNPROFOR representatives had insisted on the signing of the agreement on cessation of hostilities in order to enable the Muslims to have a reprieve and to gain time to regroup and supply themselves with weapons, ammunition and equipment to continue their bloody campaign, are unfortunately becoming reality." [Interpretation] And in the next passage, double standards are mentioned, and so on and so forth. Do you remember that this letter came to your hands, though it was sent to Zagreb but also to you and General De Lapresle for your information? Do you remember the crisis surrounding these events?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you I remember the events and I remember the general sentiment of those -- of those -- of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1023, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 1D3187. 1D3187.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The date is the 3rd of March. Once again, a letter from General Mladic for General Smith. And it says that he believes that a meeting of the Joint Commission will not be held on the 10th of March either, because the Muslim side is obstructing the agreement. "For the past two months, they have been performing offensive operations, without being publicly held to account for it ..." And so on. And then the next sentence says: "On the contrary, the international community and UNPROFOR have tolerated violations of the agreement and have rewarded the Muslims, secretly arming them during the cessation of hostilities by allowing a pirate aircraft to land at the airport in Tuzla under the escort and protection of NATO planes, which was also recorded by UNPROFOR on the 10th, the 12th, the 17th, the 23rd and the 24th of February, 1995." Are you aware that on these five days, the UNPROFOR registered violations of the no-fly zone in the area around the Tuzla Airport?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was those days or not, no. And I'm -- I don't -- I'm not surprised at this letter, but I don't remember this particular exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the last paragraph, it says here -- or, rather, the penultimate one, that: "As you know from daily reports, the Muslims violate the provisions of the comprehensive cease-fire agreement ..." And that since the 23rd of December until the 2nd of March, 1995, they committed 803 violations. The following paragraph says that the front-line has moved and that they took some of our territories in the vicinity of Bihac and so on. Do you remember that they had some successes in the middle of the cessation of hostilities and that they took control of some of our villages?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I -- I remember that fighting was developing during that time, and I remember that there were some of those incidents and they were carried out by the Bosnian government forces. But I'm -- I couldn't -- no, I just don't know whether it was on those days or in those places.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll show the map of their advances later on. It is not our map, but a US one. Thank you, General. Could this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1024, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 65 ter 12301. 65 ter 12301, please. Has it been admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P2256.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So much the better. Could we please have a look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is, as you can see, the regular combat report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, dated the 12th of March, 1995, where it is reported about numerous attacks within the Sarajevo zone. Can we please go back to the previous page. Yes, that's it. You can see that in the zone of responsibility of these brigades of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the cease-fire was violated permanently with regrouping, digging the trenches. And can we now please have a look at the last page. One more, please. Please have a look at item number 8, "Conclusion." "The enemy is active --" "Conclusions, estimates and decisions: "The enemy is active in different places with different sorts of weapons, regardless of the presence of UN units. The enemy does not select its targets, which is especially characteristic for the urban parts of town where they even kill children. "Continued intensive activities, increased engineering works, movements and re-deployments are to be expected. "The decision to use the SRK units has not been changed and the SRK command and brigades organs are engaged in preventing the enemy activities and losses." Does this look to you like offensive operations conducted in the middle of a cease-fire, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly active operations. What the objective of these were and whether they were carrying out an offence or merely conducting a series of minor attacks along their front-line, I've got no way of measuring on one -- on one situation report. But certainly fighting is being reported.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We now please see P2248. It's a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my memo sent to the Government of Republika Srpska, the presidents of municipalities, and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It says: "Pursuant to," which laws, "and in order to successfully stop the enemy offensive and conduct a counter-offensive, I hereby order:" And the measures are then enumerated which the civilian authorities should take in order to ensure that people and assets are mobilised in order to prevent and stop the enemy offensive, and to launch the counter-offensive in those areas where we had lost some territories. So the four-month cease-fire did not end, and we were forced to mobilise all the forces we had, including even workers, to defend ourselves from this offensive. This was issued on the 26th of March, and do you remember that as early as in March, this offensive launched by the BiH Army was already well underway? Do you remember that, General, because these activities of theirs had become an offensive, so much so that we had to use and mobilise all our forces, even our civilian sector, so that they would help the army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember being shown this letter a couple of days ago, and I remember that the Bosnian government had conducted two large attacks during March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? Oh, sorry, this is already an exhibit. Can we now see 65 ter 10616.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram of the UNPROFOR, dated 18 March 1995. And below, under "Highlights," it lists various topics: "The parties to the conflict openly express willingness to return to war ..." "The grip around the enclaves is tightening, the blue routes and the air bridge are closed and convoys are problematic." Number 3: "Friends of the Federation meeting produces $300 million in pledges." And: "Tudjman's announcement that the UN can remain in Croatia prompts Karadzic to reject control of the RS-RSK border by the UN." Can we now see page 5 of this document. Paragraph 12, the last two sentences: [In English] "The US, the EU and other friends announced pledges of US dollars 300 million in support of the Federation. There was also talk by US officials, though as of yet no confirmation, that the government was going to send a retired military official to advise the Federation army on military matters." [Interpretation] Do you know that at that moment, we were under triple sanctions; the embargo of the international community, an embargo imposed by Yugoslavia, and we could expect nothing better from the Federation or Croatia? We were completely blocked, and here the friends of the Federation offer $300 million plus experts to help their army. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that -- they say they discuss it. They don't -- it's not being offered -- I beg your pardon. They discuss the retired military official. They don't say they're going to provide him. But I didn't know about it in those terms as spread out there. That -- that there was US support for the Federation, I did know, but not in those -- in that detail, in those terms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this has been also admitted as Exhibit P2257.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 65 ter 3888, P2261. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 22nd April, three months into your tenure, and this is a meeting in Sarajevo and in Pale, first a meeting with Bosnian government officials. First of all, General, I must say that this -- these terms, "Bosnian government" and "Bosnian Serbs," are unfair, because from the beginning we were equal parties to the conflict. Do you know that we had that status of equal parties to the conflict, and they could not have possibly been the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Never mind. I withdraw that. It doesn't matter. What matters is that they are -- we are being treated as rebels, although we started off as equal parties to the conflict. Let's quote from here: "The BH official sounded criticised COHA, the UNPROFOR mandate, and the situation at Sarajevo Airport. On the subject of an extension of the COHA, Silajdzic maintained that any extension was not in their interest, the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement ..." And so on. Do you see that the Muslim side was against the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement and they said it was not in their interest?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Silajdzic was saying it, and he was part of their leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we never said we were in favour of breaking that agreement, that cease-fire; on the contrary, we often protested because the other side was breaking it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember -- "do you agree that we never said we were in favour of breaking that agreement." I don't remember you saying that you were in favour of breaking the agreement, but I'm equally not clear that that's what they're saying in this paragraph. He's talking about an extension of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if I read this correctly, Silajdzic maintained that any extension of that cease-fire or cessation of hostilities was not in their interests. That's in paragraph 2. And a few days before, less than a month before, they had started a major offensive in end March. Doesn't this clearly say that Silajdzic maintained it was not in their interest to extend the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that, yes: "Silajdzic maintained that any extension was not in their interest."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see what Karadzic says, paragraph 8: [In English] "When the matter of extension of COHA was raised, Karadzic retorted that it has been breached so massively by the Muslims that it does not exist. He asserted that the agreement had simply given the B and H the opportunity to rearm and reorganise, and, 'The Serbs will no longer enter into agreements which would be detrimental to ourselves.'" [Interpretation] Do you agree, then, it was our position that that agreement was never really in effect, as far as the Muslim side is concerned, and they used cease-fires for regrouping and rearming, and that was at our expense, to our detriment?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're quoted as saying is that it didn't exist anymore and that you certainly didn't want to extend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not that we didn't want to extend it. It's that we don't see any use in agreements that they would not honour, but instead use to get stronger. The reason why we didn't want to extend it is that they were using it to their advantage. Was that my position?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you were saying there, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. Paragraph 9, second sentence: [In English] "Karadzic denied responsibility for attacks on UNPROFOR personnel, but accepted that there had been mistakes." [Interpretation] Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find -- which paragraph are we in, I'm sorry, paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Nine, third line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the specific point, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted? It's already an exhibit. Thank you. 65 ter 18972, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, let me try to refresh your memory, General. General Mladic always said, If our renegades or individuals from our side attack the UNPROFOR at any time, the UNPROFOR is free to retaliate. And I was always saying that our army was not doing that in an organised manner, and if any incidents happened, we would investigate. Let's see this document, where the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska -- it's a strictly confidential document dated 12 March, 1995, sent to all corps. It's first a piece of information, followed by an order. And then it says -- there is a passage where: "The Army of Republika Srpska and its Main Staff, as well as other institutions in Republika Srpska, have many objections to the biased behaviour of UNPROFOR members which is frequently discussed at meetings held with UNPROFOR representatives. We firmly believe that these United Nations forces should be given full support in carrying out their tasks." And then further down it says: "In the past also, there have been cases of robbery against members of the UNPROFOR, but such cases have become more frequent in the past months, especially in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. There were cases of groups of armed and masked men stopping UNPROFOR vehicles and taking their vehicles, weapons and personal effects at gunpoint." And now the last paragraph, if we can scroll down: "Such and similar acts --" It's on the next page, maybe: "Such and similar acts of robbery constitute the crime of robbery under Article 150 ..." And so on and so on. "... entailing a sentence of minimum five-year imprisonment ..." Et cetera. And: "Because of all the above, I hereby order: "1. Engaging all available forces ..." Et cetera, et cetera. We can look at this entire order, a secret document whereby it is very strictly ordered to respect the status of the UNPROFOR, to engage security organs and military police to investigate such incidents, recover stolen property, et cetera, and I will personally take appropriate measures against the corps commanders in whose zones of responsibilities such acts happen. Do you see from this that General Mladic, indeed, ordered any such incidents to be strictly punished?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1025, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see briefly P2263 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was written by one of your officers, Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter. The date is 1st May 1995, and then there is a subheading "Meeting with Bosnian government officials." Mr. Akashi, General Smith and General Janvier met Dr. Ganic and Ambassador Sacirbey. The topic was the extension of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. Next page, please. There it is. [In English] "Although the criticism was not personalised, the meeting was a clear attempt to dramatise the situation in Sarajevo and to denounce the failure of UNPROFOR to respond in a forceful and punitive manner against the Bosnian Serb siege of Sarajevo and Bosnian control of Sarajevo Airport." [Interpretation] Was this pressure by the Bosnian government, the pressure that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an example of their continual theme of our relationships with that group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And their purpose and their wish was to have you fighting against the Serbs for them and to punish the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as the Bosnian Serbs wanted us to act against the Bosnian government forces, so it applied in the other direction. Both parties were -- had this theme in our relationships together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Except we didn't want you to fight for us. We only wanted you to caution and punish them as you cautioned and punished us, whereas they wanted you to create a state for them, to wage war on their behalf. You are aware, aren't you, that the Bosnian Muslim side tried, throughout the war, to involve NATO into that war on their side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you before I'm a -- I was a UN officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at this meeting with Bosnian Serb officials: [In English] "A meeting was held at Pale between Mr. Akashi and Dr. Karadzic. Karadzic's party included Krajisnik ..." [Interpretation] And so on. And it says: [In English] "He referred, however, to the situation in Sector West and claimed the Croats had attacked RSK territory and had shelled two Bosnian Serb towns. He stated that the BSA would retaliate, but that the retaliation would be directed at military targets only." [Interpretation] Do you recall, General, that on that day, on the 30th of April, and the 1st of May, Croatia took the rest of Western Slavonia and the rest of Sector West, and many Serbs fled to Republika Srpska as refugees?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I couldn't be certain of the dates, but I remember the event, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this already an exhibit? It is. Can we now see 1D3189.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, that on the 15th of May, the Muslims started that offensive that lasted until the end of May and spilled over into June? We remember it all, but they started their offensive on the 15th of May, and the 16th of May, Professor Koljevic, president for the State Committee for Co-operation with the United Nations and International Humanitarian Organisations, is addressing this letter to Yasushi Akashi, saying that: "The Serb side is quite prepared to reopen Sarajevo Airport at the earliest possible date ..." And in the last paragraph: "Moreover, given the overall deterioration of the military situation in the region of Sarajevo, the Serb side is ready to meet the other side in the conflict on the highest level of political representation. We thus hope it will be possible to prevent the escalation of current military activities." Do you agree that this is a last-ditch, desperate attempt by Professor Koljevic to prevent such an escalation by offering to reopen the airport?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's certainly making that offer. I'm -- I don't know that it's a last-ditch attempt. And you asked me if I remembered, and put all this in relation to a Bosnian government offensive. And as I've said before, I can't recall the dates, but somewhere around the middle of May, there is an up-surge of fighting in the vicinity of Sarajevo. And that may be connected with this, the reference to the deterioration in the military situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? I want to show just one more document on this topic, and then we'll be done for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1026, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3165.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting: General, you do remember who Aleksandar Ivanko is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was from his press briefing. But lower down: "84 explosions were reported yesterday, mainly in Nedzarici." And then it goes on to say: "In the area of the airport, Igman/Butmir, Halilovici, Sharpstone, and the red building ..." And so on. [In English] "The UN camp at Zetra went to state red for several hours from 10.30 yesterday. After 6.00, 120 mortar rounds impacted in the vicinity." [Interpretation] And towards the end, it is: "It is thought the BSA are targeting Zetra because of the BH Army firing point close to the camp ..." [In English] "A number of the protests at the highest level have been sent to BH." [Interpretation] Do you agree that on the 22nd May, it had already been seven days of this, and only then did the Serbs respond, and that's when the UNPROFOR sent a protest to the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that's correct, that it went on for seven days and the very first response was on this -- is reported in this press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is an authentic document from a press briefing given by a spokesman.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not questioning the document. You've shown me a document. I think it was dated the 16th or 15th. And you're now showing me one of the 22nd. I'm -- the first one says that there was a deteriorating situation, which I agreed I could remember, but I couldn't agree the dates. And you're now showing me one dated six or seven days later which reports the events of the previous 24 hours, and I'm -- I can't make the connections you're asking me to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is the connection: We agreed they started their offensive in mid-May. On the 22nd of May, the spokesman of your command holds a press briefing, informing that shells fell on Nedzarici, a Serbian neighbourhood, they also fell on Sharpstone, which is the Serbian defence line, and that the Serbs responded by fire on Zetra. I'm just trying to come to the moment, and we will come to that tomorrow, the end of May and that crisis. The Muslim offensive is going on at full blast, and it's an exchange of fire. It's a week before the bombing campaign started.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you asked me was that -- to say -- to agree with you that it took seven days for the Serbs to respond, and I am not agreeing with you that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave that aside. I don't know when we responded, but we responded by fire against Zetra on this day. Do you agree that an offensive was underway and that your spokesman was well aware that shelling was targeting Nedzarici, a Serbian neighbourhood, and Sharpstone as well, and that the UNPROFOR sent numerous protests to the highest level of the Bosnian leadership? Is that written in the last sentence here?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am entirely content to agree to what is written in that last two paragraphs of that page you've got on the screen, the one beginning with "84 detonations," and the other one, "Two civilians were killed." If that's what you're asking me, then I'm content that my spokesman would have said what he thought was happening or had happened in the last 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. That will be it for today. It has been a very long day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I appreciate the indulgence of the staff members as well as General Smith. For planning purpose, Mr. Karadzic, it would be better to know in advance, but whether it is possible at all that you conclude your cross-examination in three sessions tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are quite a few subjects we have to cover; the imprisonment, the enclaves, the convoys, all the things that the general mentioned and on which documents are led. I'm very concerned about the statements of all the witnesses. I don't know how the Trial Chamber will treat them. But when we come to specific examples, we can easily deal with them. Generalised witness statements are a great threat to me. But I hope we will finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 11th day of February, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.36 p.m.,
